summary: Research true, current tool stacks and non-trivial work stories for five engineering personas, refute them, then propose distinct diagram concepts

research.persona: Senior/staff analytics engineer (data engineer who owns data products end to end). Sits between the source systems and the people who make decisions on the numbers. Owns a warehouse or lakehouse layer, the transformation repo, the semantic/metric definitions, the contracts that downstream consumers depend on, and the on-call rota for the pipelines. Ships through pull requests against a dbt (or Spark/SQL) repo, promotes through dev/staging/prod environments, and is accountable when a finance figure changes without anyone deciding it should. Often the only person in the org who can say authoritatively what a number means, where it came from, and whether last quarter's version of it still reproduces. Works fluently in SQL, Python, YAML and Git, but the actual job is grain, semantics, history and reconciliation, not writing SELECT statements.
research.seniority_marker: A competent analytics engineer makes the new number correct. A top-level one makes the OLD number reproducible while the new one lands, and can prove the two agree wherever they should. Concretely: they treat grain and history as the primary design artifacts, not the SQL; they publish a change as a versioned model alongside the old one with a reconciliation test rather than an in-place ALTER; they know which of their reconciliations is an independent derivation and which is the same logic run twice (and refuse to count the latter as verification); they pin the snapshot the comparison runs against so the test is deterministic; and they sequence the retirement of the old version against observed consumer traffic rather than an announcement. The tell is that they can answer "what would have to be true for this figure to be wrong?" with a specific query, and they have already run it.

story.title: Re-graining the order fact table from header to line item, with six consumers on it and five years of history that no longer exists at source
story.narrative:
fct_orders was one row per order. Finance needed line-item margin, so the grain had to move to one row per order line, and net_revenue had to keep summing to the identical value for every closed period back to 2021. Six things depended on it: two Power BI semantic models, a Looker Explore, a churn feature table, a partner-facing Snowflake secure share, and a nightly reverse-ETL job.

The design decision was to publish v2 as a separate dbt model beside v1, never an in-place change. The hard part was history: the source overwrote discount allocations in place, so line-level history was simply gone. Reconstruction came from three seams stitched together, a dbt snapshot that only began in 2023, Snowflake Time Travel (Enterprise caps at 90 days, so useless for 2021), and an archived Iceberg export of the raw extracts. A bridge model allocates header discount to lines by pre-discount amount, with a test that fails if any allocation is non-exhaustive by more than a cent.

Verification ran against a zero-copy clone of production: a reconciliation test that fails when any month's net_revenue differs by more than 0.005 percent, plus a second, independently written derivation in Snowpark against a pinned snapshot. The PR built only the changed subgraph via state:modified+ with --defer into a PR-scoped schema. The ODCS contract was bumped to v2 with the grain change declared, and v1 stayed live until a Snowflake Data Metric Function showed its query count at zero for a full close cycle.
story.why_not_trivial: The SQL is the easy part. The difficulty is that the grain being asked for never existed in the source, so history has to be reconstructed from three incomplete seams and then defended as an allocation choice rather than a fact. On top of that, equivalence has to be proven for every closed accounting period against consumers the engineer does not own and cannot atomically change, which forces a versioned coexistence and a traffic-driven retirement rather than a cutover. A junior can write the line-level model in an afternoon; nobody junior can decide what 2021 line-level discount means, prove the restated totals tie out, and sequence six consumers off the old table without a finance restatement.

tools.name: Snowflake (Time Travel, zero-copy cloning, Streams, Tasks, Dynamic Tables, Snowpark, Iceberg tables)
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Primary warehouse. Time Travel (AT/BEFORE with TIMESTAMP, OFFSET or STATEMENT; up to 90 days on Enterprise, 1 day on Standard, then Fail-safe) and zero-copy clones give you a pinned, restorable snapshot to reconcile against. Streams plus Tasks for hand-controlled CDC with MERGE and custom retry; Dynamic Tables for declarative incremental refresh where you do not need that control. Snowpark for Python/DataFrame logic that runs in the warehouse. Iceberg tables and the Iceberg REST Catalog API for open-format storage.

tools.name: Snowflake Horizon Catalog
tools.what_it_is_used_for: The governance and catalog layer: end-to-end lineage, object tagging, sensitive data classification, data protection policies, access history, Trust Center, Internal Marketplace, semantic views, and catalog-linked databases. Snowflake now positions it as an 'agentic catalog' covering data inside and outside Snowflake.

tools.name: Snowflake Data Metric Functions (DMFs)
tools.what_it_is_used_for: SQL-native data quality monitoring attached to tables and columns. System DMFs in SNOWFLAKE.CORE cover freshness, row count, duplicate count, null count; custom DMFs cover domain rules. Results are stored and can drive alerts. Requires Enterprise Edition. Useful for measuring consumer traffic and quality on a table you are trying to deprecate.

tools.name: Snowflake Openflow
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Managed multi-modal ingestion (batch, streaming, CDC, structured and unstructured), built on Apache NiFi from the Datavolo acquisition. Deploys in a Snowflake-managed VPC via Snowpark Container Services or in your own cloud VPC. Deployment-option availability varies by cloud, so check the matrix before designing around it.

tools.name: Databricks Lakeflow pipelines (the product formerly called Delta Live Tables / DLT)
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Declarative ETL pipelines. The rename is real and load-bearing for anyone writing docs: Databricks' own page is titled 'What happened to Delta Live Tables (DLT)?' and states DLT is now Lakeflow pipelines, with no migration required. Python API changes: `import dlt` becomes `from pyspark import pipelines as dp`; `@table` now creates streaming tables; new `@materialized_view`; `@view` becomes `@temporary_view`. Classic SKUs still start with DLT and event log schemas still say dlt, which is a common source of confusion. Aligns with Apache Spark Declarative Pipelines from Spark 4.1.

tools.name: Databricks Unity Catalog (with Managed Iceberg, Foreign Iceberg, Delta Sharing)
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Governance, lineage and permissions across catalogs/schemas/tables/volumes/models. As of 2026: Managed Iceberg is GA (create, read, write, optimize, govern, share Iceberg in UC with Predictive Optimization and Liquid Clustering); Iceberg v3 is GA with deletion vectors, row tracking and VARIANT across managed, foreign and UniForm tables; Foreign Iceberg with credential vending is GA; external sharing to Iceberg REST clients over the Delta Sharing protocol is GA. Cross-engine ABAC is Beta. Catalog federation connectors include AWS Glue, Snowflake Horizon, Hive Metastore, Salesforce, plus newer Google Cloud and Palantir.

tools.name: Databricks Asset Bundles (DABs)
tools.what_it_is_used_for: YAML-defined deployment unit that ships jobs, pipelines, notebooks, dashboards and MLflow experiments together, with per-target (dev/staging/prod) configuration. This is the mechanism that makes environment promotion from GitHub Actions or Azure Pipelines deterministic and stops the classic drift where code ships but the job definition does not. Pairs with OIDC federation so CI authenticates without long-lived PATs.

tools.name: Databricks SQL and MLflow
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Databricks SQL for the warehouse-style serving layer and BI connections; MLflow for experiment tracking, model registry (registered in Unity Catalog) and evaluation. Both are addressable as resources inside a Databricks Asset Bundle.

tools.name: dbt (dbt Core v2, dbt Fusion engine, dbt platform)
tools.what_it_is_used_for: The transformation layer and the thing the PR is actually about: models, tests, unit tests, snapshots, exposures, contracts, `dbt build`, `state:modified+` and `--defer` for Slim CI. Two naming facts to get right in 2026: dbt Cloud is now called the dbt platform, and the Rust-based dbt Fusion engine is the engine behind dbt v2 with the code published into dbt-core under Apache 2.0 (announced June 2026). Fusion adapter status is still per-warehouse: Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks and Redshift at Preview; Spark and DuckDB at Beta (CLI only). Do not describe Fusion as fully GA everywhere.

tools.name: Apache Airflow 3.3
tools.vendor: Apache Software Foundation (managed as Astro by Astronomer, MWAA by AWS, Cloud Composer by Google)
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Orchestration. Airflow 3 brought asset-centric scheduling, DAG versioning, a React UI and improved backfills. 3.1 added human-in-the-loop workflows and deadline alerts. 3.3 (released 6 July 2026) added a task state store for stateful tasks that persist key-value state across retries and runs, a Language Task SDK letting task bodies be written in Java or Go while orchestration stays Python, asset partition mappers (FanOutMapper, FixedKeyMapper) and per-run control over which bundle version a cleared or backfilled run uses.

tools.name: Dagster 1.13 (Components, dg CLI, Dagster+)
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Asset-first orchestration. 1.13 (9 April 2026, 'Octopus's Garden') shipped partitioned asset checks, state-backed Components on by default (dbt, Fivetran, Airbyte, BI metadata without constant re-querying), Virtual Assets in preview, expanded `dg api` for jobs/runs/schedules/sensors/deployments, and 20+ new Components. The dg CLI plus YAML Components is now the standard local dev entry point.

tools.name: Great Expectations (GX Core, GX Cloud)
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Python validation framework: Expectations, Checkpoints, Data Docs. GX Core is the open source package, GX Cloud the managed layer. Used where validation has to live outside the warehouse or cover files/dataframes rather than tables.

tools.name: Soda (Soda Core, SodaCL, Soda Cloud)
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Declarative YAML checks (SodaCL) run from a CLI, with Soda Cloud for monitoring, alerting and anomaly detection. Positioned toward business-facing data contracts where non-engineers need to see contract health.

tools.name: Elementary
tools.what_it_is_used_for: The usual first step into observability for dbt-native teams: installs as a dbt package, stores test result history, adds anomaly detection and a self-hosted report, with Elementary Cloud as the hosted tier. Cheap way to get trend data on tests you already have.

tools.name: Monte Carlo
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Managed data observability: automated freshness/volume/schema monitors, incident management, field-level lineage across warehouse, lakehouse and BI. The enterprise-tier answer where the org wants coverage without writing every check.

tools.name: Open Data Contract Standard (ODCS) v3.1.0
tools.what_it_is_used_for: The open standard for writing a data contract: schema, quality rules, SLAs, stakeholders, roles. v3.1.0 added relationships between properties, stricter JSON Schema validation, richer metadata and executable SLAs, and is backward compatible with v3.0. This is the artifact you version when a grain changes, and the thing a merge gate can mechanically check.

tools.name: DataHub / DataHub Cloud
tools.vendor: DataHub (the company formerly named Acryl Data; rebranded May 2025)
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Open source metadata platform and catalog with column-level lineage, ingestion connectors and a managed DataHub Cloud tier. Name check matters: 'Acryl Data' is stale, though the PyPI package is still `acryl-datahub`.

tools.name: OpenMetadata
tools.what_it_is_used_for: The other major open source catalog: discovery, lineage, quality tests and governance, with Collate offering the managed SaaS version. Usually evaluated head-to-head against DataHub.

tools.name: Power BI semantic models with PBIP and TMDL, Fabric Git integration, Deployment Pipelines, fabric-cicd
tools.what_it_is_used_for: The BI end of the contract. TMDL is the text format for semantic models; PBIP is the project folder format that makes models and reports diffable in Git. Fabric Git integration syncs a workspace to Azure DevOps or GitHub; Deployment Pipelines handle dev/test/prod promotion; `fabric-cicd` is Microsoft's open source Python library over the Fabric REST APIs for code-first deployment, with `fab deploy` in the Fabric CLI as the alternative. Tabular Editor's Best Practice Analyzer is the common quality gate in build validation.

tools.name: Looker (LookML) and Tableau
tools.what_it_is_used_for: The other two semantic/BI surfaces a data product typically has to satisfy. LookML is version-controlled in Git and is the place a metric definition silently diverges from the dbt definition. Tableau workbooks and published data sources are the classic consumer that is hardest to inventory when you deprecate a table.

tools.name: Apache Iceberg (v3) and Delta Lake
tools.vendor: Apache Software Foundation; Linux Foundation / Databricks
tools.what_it_is_used_for: The two table formats that actually matter in 2026. Iceberg v3 (deletion vectors, row tracking, VARIANT) is GA on both Snowflake and Databricks, and both vendors now expose Iceberg REST catalog APIs and credential vending, so cross-engine reads without a rewrite are real. The interoperability is genuinely contested marketing territory: Databricks claims Unity Catalog is the most interoperable Iceberg catalog, Snowflake claims Horizon has fuller bidirectional REST support. Apache Hudi still exists but is a distant third in this stack and rarely the default choice for new work.

tools.name: GitHub (Actions, rulesets/branch protection, CODEOWNERS, required checks)
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Where the data PR lives. A real data PR contains: the model SQL/Python, its schema YAML with tests and contract, an updated ODCS contract file if the interface changed, a migration or backfill script with a documented reverse path, the CI run showing a Slim CI build against a PR-scoped schema, and the reconciliation output pasted into the PR body. Actions runs `dbt build` with `state:modified+ --defer`, the linters, and the bundle/deploy step. CODEOWNERS routes semantic-layer and contract files to their owners; required status checks and rulesets are what actually block the merge.

tools.name: Azure DevOps Repos and Azure Pipelines
tools.what_it_is_used_for: The common alternative in Microsoft-shop data teams, and it behaves differently from GitHub in ways that change how gates are built. Branch policies are configured per-branch on the server rather than as a file in the repo (no CODEOWNERS file); the equivalent of CODEOWNERS is 'Automatically included reviewers', the one branch policy that supports path filters. Build validation policies queue a pipeline on PR create and on every push, and you can require several independently (CI plus a security scan). Merge strategy, comment resolution and linked work items are enforceable policies. Practical consequence: policy is centrally administered and not reviewable in the PR diff, so a BrotherSBE-style merge gate has to be asserted as a pipeline step rather than a repo file.

tools.name: SQLFluff
tools.what_it_is_used_for: SQL linter and formatter with a dbt templater, run in CI so style and anti-pattern rules are mechanical rather than argued about in review. Frequently paired with pre-commit and dbt-checkpoint style repo hygiene checks.

tools.name: Microsoft Fabric Data Factory / Azure Data Factory
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Ingestion and pipeline orchestration in Azure estates. Worth being precise in 2026: Microsoft has moved primary development to Fabric Data Factory, new capabilities such as mirroring and copy jobs are shipping there and are not being backported to classic Azure Data Factory, and a migration assistant for ADF and Synapse pipelines went to public preview in March 2026. Calling classic ADF the current product is a dated claim.

rituals: Pull request as the unit of change: no transformation reaches production except through a PR, with the CI build log and the reconciliation output pasted into the PR body rather than summarized.

Slim CI on every PR: `dbt build` with `state:modified+` and `--defer` against the production manifest, materializing into a PR-scoped schema that is dropped on merge. Cost and runtime are part of the review.

Environment promotion dev to staging to prod expressed as configuration, not as a manual step: dbt targets, Databricks Asset Bundle targets, Fabric Deployment Pipelines. Nobody clicks in a production workspace.
CODEOWNERS (or Azure Repos 'automatically included reviewers' with path filters) routing semantic-layer files, contract files and anything touching finance-facing marts to named owners.
Data contract review: an ODCS contract is versioned alongside the model, and a grain, type or nullability change forces a contract bump and a consumer notification before merge.
Design doc / ADR before any grain, key or partitioning change, recording the alternatives and what would reverse the decision. Filed in the Obsidian vault, linked from the PR.
Backfill runbook written before the backfill runs: idempotency argument, batch size, expected cost, how to tell it is half-done, and the exact reverse command. Reviewed by a second person.

Reconciliation ritual: any restated figure gets a second derivation written by someone other than the model author, against a pinned snapshot, and the two are compared before the number is shown to anyone.

Freshness and quality checks as first-class code: dbt tests plus Snowflake DMFs or Soda/GX checks, with results trended (Elementary or Monte Carlo) so a slow drift is visible rather than only a hard failure.
Deprecation with evidence: an old model stays live until query-log telemetry shows zero consumer reads for a full business cycle, then is dropped, never on an announcement date alone.
On-call rotation for pipelines with a written incident timeline in the vault, including which downstream numbers were wrong and for how long, and who was told.

Weekly lineage and exposure review before any schema change, using Unity Catalog / Horizon / DataHub lineage plus dbt exposures, on the assumption that the inventory of consumers is always incomplete.
Cost review as part of code review: warehouse credits or DBU delta for the change, because a correct model that triples the bill is not merged.

failure_modes.what_goes_wrong: A join fan-out after a grain change silently duplicates rows, so an additive measure such as revenue or units is overstated. The classic version: the new line-level fact is joined to a dimension that is not unique on the join key, or an SCD2 dimension is joined without a validity-window predicate, so one fact row matches two versions of the same entity.
failure_modes.why_it_is_silent: Nothing errors. Row counts are expected to change because the grain changed, so the usual smell test is unavailable. Standard tests (not_null, unique on a surrogate key, accepted_values) all still pass, because the duplicated rows each have valid values and a distinct generated key. The total only looks wrong to someone who already knows what it should be, and by the time finance notices, several closed periods have been published.
failure_modes.how_ai_assistance_makes_it_worse: An assistant will happily write the join and a plausible-looking set of tests, and will assert the model is correct without ever computing the pre-change and post-change totals. It has no access to the ground truth figure and no instinct that a grain change demands a sum-preservation proof, so it substitutes a confident summary for a reconciliation. It will also reach for SELECT DISTINCT or a QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() to make the duplicate warning go away, which hides the fan-out permanently instead of fixing the join. This is exactly the case BrotherSBE's numbers gate is for: absent a second derivation against a pinned snapshot, the figure is NO-DATA, not a pass.

failure_modes.what_goes_wrong: An incremental model's predicate window quietly excludes late-arriving or back-dated records. The model filters on an event timestamp with something like `where updated_at > (select max(updated_at) from this)`, and rows that arrive days late, or are back-dated by an upstream correction, are never picked up.
failure_modes.why_it_is_silent: The pipeline succeeds every night. Row counts grow. Freshness checks pass because recent data is present. The gap only exists in a historical window nobody is looking at, and the next full refresh silently repairs it, which also destroys the evidence. Dev environments are usually full-refreshed, so CI never executes the incremental code path that contains the bug.
failure_modes.how_ai_assistance_makes_it_worse: Incremental predicates are one of the most confidently generated and least verified pieces of code an assistant produces, because the pattern is extremely common in training data and looks right. The assistant cannot see the source system's late-arrival behavior, so it defaults to the naive high-water-mark form. It will also validate the model by running a full refresh, which passes, and report success, because the failing path is the one CI never runs.

failure_modes.what_goes_wrong: Reconstructed history in a slowly changing dimension is fabricated rather than derived. When source history has been overwritten, effective_from and effective_to dates get inferred from whatever seam is available (a snapshot that only starts partway through, a file arrival date, a load timestamp), and those inferences get presented as facts. Downstream point-in-time joins then attribute activity to the wrong segment, region or price band for the reconstructed period.
failure_modes.why_it_is_silent: The dimension passes every structural test you would write for an SCD2: no overlapping validity windows, no gaps, exactly one current record per key, referential integrity intact. It is internally consistent and externally wrong. The error surfaces years later as an unexplainable cohort trend that everyone assumes is a real business effect.
failure_modes.how_ai_assistance_makes_it_worse: Asked to 'reconstruct history', an assistant produces a well-formed SCD2 with plausible dates and no annotation that the dates are inferred. It fills the gap because filling the gap is what it was asked to do, and a fluent answer is indistinguishable from a sourced one in the output. The correct behavior, refusing to date rows that have no evidence and marking that span NO-DATA, is the behavior that looks like failure. The assistant will also write the structural tests that pass, which reinforces the false confidence.

failure_modes.what_goes_wrong: Metric definitions drift between the transformation layer and the semantic layer. `net_revenue` is defined in a dbt model, again as a DAX measure in a Power BI semantic model, again in a LookML measure, and again in a hand-written export query. One of them is updated when the business rule changes; the others are not.
failure_modes.why_it_is_silent: Every system is internally consistent and every dashboard renders. There is no shared assertion connecting the four definitions, so nothing compares them. The divergence only appears when two people bring numbers to the same meeting, and even then it is usually attributed to different filters or date ranges rather than to different definitions.
failure_modes.how_ai_assistance_makes_it_worse: An assistant asked to add or change a measure will edit the one file it was pointed at and will not go looking for the other three surfaces, because they live in other repos, other file formats, or a BI tool it cannot see. It optimizes for the local edit looking complete. Worse, it will write a confident summary saying the metric has been updated, with no caveat that only one of four definitions was touched.

failure_modes.what_goes_wrong: A migration or backfill has no tested reverse path. The forward script runs, partially completes, and there is no way back: the source rows have been overwritten, the old table has been dropped, or the reverse script exists but has never been executed against anything resembling production.
failure_modes.why_it_is_silent: The reverse path is not silent so much as untested-and-assumed. It reads as done because a `down` script sits in the repo next to the `up` script. Nobody discovers it does not work until it is being run in an incident, on the worst night, against a table that no longer has Time Travel coverage because the retention window has already passed.
failure_modes.how_ai_assistance_makes_it_worse: Assistants reliably produce a forward migration and a syntactically valid reverse migration, and just as reliably never run the reverse one. The pair looks complete on inspection. The assistant also has no model of retention windows (Snowflake Time Travel is 90 days maximum on Enterprise and one day on Standard, then Fail-safe, where the data is unqueryable) so it will assume recovery is always available. This is precisely the migration gate: forward and reverse both have to run against a restored copy, and a reverse script that has never executed is NO-DATA.

failure_modes.what_goes_wrong: The consumer inventory is incomplete when a table is changed or dropped. Lineage tools capture dbt refs, warehouse query history and BI connections, but miss the reverse-ETL job authenticating as a service account, the secure share to a partner, the notebook someone scheduled, and the CSV export in a finance macro.
failure_modes.why_it_is_silent: Lineage graphs render beautifully and look authoritative, which is exactly the problem: a complete-looking picture suppresses the instinct to go check the query log. The missed consumer fails quietly or, worse, keeps returning stale data from a cached or replicated copy, so nobody reports an outage at all.
failure_modes.how_ai_assistance_makes_it_worse: An assistant will read the lineage graph or the dbt manifest, enumerate the dependents it finds, and present that list as the impact analysis without flagging it as a lower bound. Its output format (a clean list of six consumers) carries an implicit claim of completeness that the underlying evidence does not support. The honest answer is 'six known consumers plus unknown direct query traffic, here is the query-log check to run', and that is not the answer that gets generated by default.

verdict.persona: Senior/staff analytics engineer who owns data products end to end: warehouse/lakehouse layer, the transformation repo, semantic and metric definitions, the consumer contracts, and the pipeline on-call. Ships through PRs, promotes dev/staging/prod as configuration, and is accountable when a finance figure moves without a decision. The persona itself survives fact-checking: it is a real, currently-staffed seat and the seniority marker (make the OLD number reproducible while the new one lands, and know which reconciliation is an independent derivation versus the same logic run twice) is the right principal-level tell. No correction needed to the persona or the story premise. Corrections below are confined to tool facts, vendor ownership, and one capability claim that cannot be executed as written.
invented_or_wrong: CAPABILITY MISATTRIBUTION (appears twice, in the story narrative and in the tool entry): 'v1 stayed live until a Snowflake Data Metric Function showed its query count at zero' and 'Useful for measuring consumer traffic on a table you are trying to deprecate'. Data Metric Functions measure attributes OF THE DATA (null count, duplicate count, row count, freshness) per docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/data-quality-intro, which describes them as measuring 'an attribute of your data such as how many NULL values exist in a column or how often a table is being updated'. There is no system DMF for consumer query traffic, and the docs do not support it. The deprecation ritual as written cannot be run. The real mechanism is SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.ACCESS_HISTORY / QUERY_HISTORY (plus Horizon lineage). This is the single most damaging error in the draft because the booklet is about evidence gates and this gate is unexecutable.

DEAD PRODUCT PRESENTED AS LIVE: 'Great Expectations (GX Core, GX Cloud) ... GX Core is the open source package, GX Cloud the managed layer'. Per greatexpectations.io/blog/an-update-from-great-expectations/ (6 May 2026), FICO acquired GX Cloud and folded it into the FICO platform, and GX Cloud ceased public availability on 1 June 2026. Fivetran became steward of the open source GX Core project. Recommending GX Cloud in an August 2026 booklet points readers at a product they cannot buy.

WRONG RELATIONSHIP: 'fabric-cicd is Microsoft's open source Python library ... with `fab deploy` in the Fabric CLI as the alternative'. They are not alternatives. Per the Fabric CLI v1.5 GA announcement, `fab deploy` wraps the fabric-cicd library under the hood. Everything else in that entry (TMDL, PBIP, Fabric Git integration, Deployment Pipelines, fabric-cicd officially Microsoft-supported since Feb 2026, Tabular Editor BPA) checks out.

UNVERIFIED AND LIKELY OVERSTATED: Azure DevOps entry claims 'Automatically included reviewers' is 'the one branch policy that supports path filters'. Build validation policies also accept path filters, so the exclusivity claim is wrong as stated. I could not re-verify against Microsoft Learn before the search budget ran out, so treat as flagged-not-proven; the surrounding point (policy is server-side and not reviewable in the PR diff, so the gate must be a pipeline step) is correct and is the part worth keeping.
stale_naming: Dagster Labs is no longer independent. Prefect announced acquisition of Dagster Labs on 13 July 2026 (dagster.io/prefect); the combined company operates under the Prefect name from August 2026. Dagster, the OSS project, and Dagster+ keep their names and remain supported, but 'vendor: Dagster Labs' is stale as of the month this booklet ships. The 1.13 'Octopus's Garden' content itself (9 April 2026, partitioned asset checks, state-backed Components default-on, Virtual Assets in preview, expanded dg api, 20+ Components) verifies clean.

dbt Labs is now part of Fivetran. The all-stock merger announced 13 Oct 2025 closed 1 June 2026, the same day dbt Core v2 and the Apache 2.0 Fusion publication were announced. The dbt brand persists, but 'vendor: dbt Labs' should read Fivetran (dbt). Second-order consequence the draft misses entirely: Fivetran now also stewards GX Core, so two separate entries in this tool list resolve to one vendor.

Soda's check language framing is one major version stale. The draft describes 'Declarative YAML checks (SodaCL)'. Soda Core 4 (first public release 28 Jan 2026) is documented as a breaking change 'moving from the checks language to a Data Contracts-based syntax', with contracts as the default way to define rules. Describing Soda as a SodaCL tool in 2026 is describing v3.
GX Cloud (see invented_or_wrong) is folded into the FICO platform; GX Core's steward is Fivetran. The name 'Great Expectations' now covers only the OSS project.

Verified NOT stale, so leave alone: Delta Live Tables to Lakeflow pipelines (confirmed on the Databricks 'Where is DLT?' page, including `import dlt` to `from pyspark import pipelines as dp`, @table now creating streaming tables, @view to @temporary_view, no migration required); Acryl Data to DataHub / DataHub Cloud (May 2025); dbt Cloud to dbt platform; Snowflake Horizon Catalog; Monte Carlo (independent, not acquired); Elementary Data; OpenMetadata/Collate; Azure Data Factory to Fabric Data Factory with the migration assistant in public preview March 2026.
overclaims: 'a Snowflake Data Metric Function showed its query count at zero for a full close cycle' overclaims DMF scope and makes the traffic-driven retirement, which is the best idea in the story, rest on a tool that cannot do it. Rewrite against ACCESS_HISTORY.

'ODCS ... the thing a merge gate can mechanically check' overstates what the standard does. ODCS is a document format (schema, quality rules, SLAs, roles); it does not execute anything. Mechanical enforcement needs a separate engine (Soda Core 4 contracts, the Data Contract CLI, or dbt tests generated from the contract). The booklet should name the engine, or the gate is a document review dressed as a check.

dbt Core v2 is real and correctly described, but note it was published as an alpha on announcement. Any sentence implying Fusion is the default production engine everywhere would overclaim; the draft's own caveat ('Do not describe Fusion as fully GA everywhere') is correct and I verified it: docs.getdbt.com/docs/fusion/fusion-availability shows Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks and Redshift at Preview and Spark and DuckDB at Beta, CLI only, with NO adapter at GA.

Snowflake Openflow: the draft hedges that 'deployment-option availability varies by cloud'. That hedge is now weaker than reality in one direction and correct in the other: Snowflake-deployed (SPCS) is GA on AWS, Azure and GCP; BYOC is GA on AWS. Keep the hedge, but it is BYOC specifically that is the constrained one.

Verified accurate, do NOT soften: Time Travel at 1 day on Standard and up to 90 days on Enterprise and higher for permanent objects, then Fail-safe where historical data is no longer queryable. The migration-gate failure mode built on this is sound. Also verified verbatim-accurate: every Airflow 3.3 claim, including the 6 July 2026 date, the task/asset state store (AIP-103), the Java and Go Language Task SDK (AIP-108), and the specific mapper names FanOutMapper and FixedKeyMapper, plus per-run bundle version control. I expected FanOutMapper/FixedKeyMapper to be the invented detail and it is not. Databricks Iceberg statuses also verify exactly: Managed Iceberg GA, Iceberg v3 GA, Foreign Iceberg with credential vending GA, external sharing to Iceberg REST clients GA, cross-engine ABAC Beta, and the federation list including Google Cloud and Palantir (the draft omits Workday).
missing_obvious_tools: Datafold. The entire draft has no value-level diffing tool, which is the exact gap between 'I wrote a reconciliation query' and 'the PR proves old and new agree row by row'. Datafold Cloud still ships data diff, monitors and column-level lineage. Hard constraint for the booklet: the open source `data-diff` package was deprecated and the repo archived on 17 May 2024, so it must NOT be offered as the free option. Datafold has also repositioned in 2026 toward AI-assisted code review and migration automation.

Recce (DataRecce). Open source plus cloud, purpose-built for exactly this story: on PR open it diffs the dev environment against production and surfaces schema changes, row counts, data diffs and downstream impact before merge. It is the closest existing product to a BrotherSBE numbers gate for dbt, and its absence from a draft whose central ritual is 'reconciliation output pasted into the PR body' is the biggest omission after Datafold.

SQLMesh / Tobiko. Now a Linux Foundation project, with Tobiko Cloud GA. Its virtual data environments give real blue-green deploys with data and instant rollback, which is a strictly stronger version of the draft's 'PR-scoped schema that is dropped on merge'. Any principal in this seat in 2026 has a considered position on SQLMesh versus dbt, and the merger of dbt Labs into Fivetran makes that position more load-bearing, not less.

A semantic layer, of any flavour. The draft names metric drift across dbt, DAX and LookML as a headline failure mode and then lists no tool that fixes it: dbt Semantic Layer / MetricFlow, Databricks metric views, Snowflake Horizon semantic views, or Cube. Diagnosing the failure and omitting the remedy is a visible hole to this audience.

Fivetran and/or Airbyte. Ingestion appears only as Openflow and Fabric Data Factory. Fivetran is also now the parent of dbt Labs and the steward of GX Core, so leaving it out of a 2026 tool list is doubly odd.

OpenLineage (and Marquez). The draft leans hard on lineage across three catalogs but never names the vendor-neutral standard that stitches them together; Snowflake Horizon explicitly ingests OpenLineage feeds into its lineage graph.
Apache Polaris, the open source Iceberg REST catalog Snowflake donated. Conspicuous in an Iceberg-heavy list that discusses REST catalogs and credential vending on both vendors.

Snowflake ACCOUNT_USAGE (ACCESS_HISTORY, QUERY_HISTORY, plus OBJECT_DEPENDENCIES). Not a product, but it is the actual evidence source for the deprecation ritual and for the 'consumer inventory is incomplete' failure mode, and it is what the DMF claim should be replaced with.

Terraform with the Snowflake provider (or Databricks provider) for warehouse objects, roles and grants. A principal owning contracts and shares provisions RBAC as code; the draft covers code promotion but not object and grant promotion.
dbt-checkpoint and pre-commit. Mentioned only in passing inside the SQLFluff entry ('dbt-checkpoint style repo hygiene'); dbt-checkpoint is a real tool and should be named as one.

Atlan, as the third name in the catalog bake-off alongside DataHub and OpenMetadata. Lower priority than the above, but it is the one an 8 to 12 person team with a governance mandate is most likely to have already bought.

research.persona: Senior backend engineer on a platform team of 8 to 12, owning two or three services in a domain (orders, billing, identity) plus the contracts those services publish to everyone else. Their real product is not endpoints, it is the interface surface: the OpenAPI document, the protobuf package, the Avro subject in the schema registry, the event envelope, the table other teams read through CDC. They spend more time on change safety than on new code: what happens during the window where old and new revisions of the same service are both serving traffic, what happens to the consumer they cannot redeploy, what the database does when an ALTER queues behind an open transaction. They write the runbook and the reverse path before the forward path. They are the person who says "that is backward compatible for the wire format, not for the generated code, and two of our consumers pin generated code" and is right. They review other people's migrations as a matter of course, own the CODEOWNERS entry for the migrations directory and the proto directory, and are usually the one who decides that a change gets split into three deploys across six weeks instead of one PR. They work in GitHub pull requests with a merge queue, they read traces before they read logs, and they treat a number without a second derivation as unproven.
research.seniority_marker: A competent engineer makes the change work. A top-level one designs the ORDER of change so that every intermediate state is correct on its own, including the states nobody plans to be in for long. Concretely: they can name, before writing code, every reader of the thing they are changing, including the ones that are not services (a partner batch job, a BI extract, a support tool, a pinned generated client), and they know which of those they can redeploy and which they cannot. They then choose a sequence where each step is independently revertible and no step depends on two deploys landing in the same hour. The second marker is that their evidence is a derived invariant, not a green pipeline: they will produce a reconciliation query whose result must match a second, independently derived figure against a pinned snapshot, and they will refuse to advance when that figure is missing rather than treating missing as fine. The third is that they actually execute the reverse path against a restored copy of production-shaped data before the forward path ships, because a down migration that has only been read is a down migration that does not exist.

story.title: Splitting an implicit-currency money column across three services and a partner settlement feed
story.narrative:
The orders table carries total_amount NUMERIC(12,2), with currency implied by the merchant's home market. Launching in Japan kills that assumption, so the column has to become total_minor BIGINT plus currency_code CHAR(3). Four readers depend on it: the orders service that writes it, a billing service reading a replica, an analytics consumer fed by CDC into a Kafka topic whose Avro schema lives in Confluent Schema Registry, and a partner's nightly settlement job that parses a positional CSV export nobody on the team controls.

The senior engineer sequences it rather than writing it. pgroll start adds the new columns, backfills roughly 400 million rows in bounded batches, and installs the two-way triggers so old and new writers stay consistent through a mixed-revision ECS window where both task definitions serve live traffic. The Avro subject gains fields with defaults under FULL_TRANSITIVE compatibility, which means the old field stays for the entire window instead of being dropped the moment a BACKWARD check goes green. The partner gets columns appended at the end of the row and a cutover date set on their release calendar, months out.

The proof is not a passing test. It is a reconciliation: total_minor summed by currency and settlement day must equal total_amount to the cent, run against a pinned snapshot and derived a second time from the CDC stream. pgroll complete runs only after tracing shows zero reads of the old column for a full billing cycle.
story.why_not_trivial: The code change is a few hundred lines. The hard part is that correctness lives in the sequence, not the diff: four readers on four independent release cadences, one of them a partner who cannot be redeployed on your schedule, and a rolling deploy that guarantees a period where both schema assumptions are live at once. The dangerous step is the one that looks safest, dropping the old column, and it is the only irreversible one. The acceptance criterion is a monetary invariant that has to hold per currency and per day across a rounding change (zero-decimal currencies multiplied by 100 are wrong), not a test suite result, and the evidence that it is safe to contract is an absence-of-traffic claim that is worthless unless the old path was instrumented first.

tools.name: Buf CLI and Buf Schema Registry (BSR)
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Protobuf and gRPC schema management. `buf breaking --against <past version>` gates PRs, with rule categories FILE, PACKAGE, WIRE_JSON and WIRE (strictest to most lenient, passing a stricter one implies the looser ones). Buf ships a GitHub Action; the BSR adds server-side breaking checks with an owner approval flow, plus generated SDKs and remote plugins.

tools.name: OpenAPI Specification 3.1 and 3.2
tools.what_it_is_used_for: REST contract definition. 3.1 aligned with JSON Schema; 3.2.0 was announced 23 September 2025 and adds explicit HTTP method support, a revised tag structure and streaming media types. Teams pin a version and lint the document in CI.

tools.name: Spectral
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Rule-based linting of OpenAPI and AsyncAPI documents in CI, so style and compatibility rules on the contract are enforced mechanically rather than in review comments.

tools.name: Pact and PactFlow
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Consumer-driven contract testing. Consumers publish pacts, providers verify them, and `can-i-deploy` answers whether a given version of a service is safe to release against what is actually deployed. PactFlow is the hosted broker and adds bi-directional contract testing (BDCT), which is not in the Pact OSS project.

tools.name: Confluent Schema Registry and Stream Governance
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Avro, Protobuf and JSON Schema subjects for Kafka topics, with compatibility levels set globally or per subject: BACKWARD, BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE, FORWARD, FORWARD_TRANSITIVE, FULL, FULL_TRANSITIVE, NONE. Data Contracts and data quality rules extend schemas with integrity constraints, migration rules, CEL and JSONata.

tools.name: Apache Kafka
tools.what_it_is_used_for: The event backbone: domain events, CDC topics, and the replay surface used to derive a figure a second way independently of the primary database query.

tools.name: Debezium
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Change data capture from Postgres logical replication into Kafka, which is how downstream analytics and reconciliation consumers see column changes without querying the OLTP database.

tools.name: Amazon EventBridge
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Event bus and routing for cross-service and SaaS integration events, with a schema registry, rules and Pipes for point-to-point transformation.

tools.name: Azure Service Bus and Azure Event Hubs
tools.what_it_is_used_for: On the Azure side of a mixed estate: Service Bus for durable queues, topics and fan-out messaging with ordering and dead-lettering; Event Hubs for high-throughput event ingestion and streaming.

tools.name: PostgreSQL
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Primary OLTP store. The senior-level surface is lock behaviour: ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on ALTER, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, adding constraints NOT VALID then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT, and lock_timeout on the migration session so a blocked DDL cannot queue the whole application behind it.

tools.name: pgroll
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Zero-downtime, reversible Postgres migrations via expand and contract. `pgroll start` creates a new virtual schema built from views over the physical tables so old and new schema versions coexist; column changes add a physical column, backfill it, and install triggers propagating writes both ways. `pgroll complete` removes the old version; `pgroll rollback` removes the new one. Single Go binary, Postgres 14+, no extension required.

tools.name: Atlas
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Declarative schema-as-code plus versioned migrations, with migration linting (`atlas migrate lint`) that flags destructive or lock-taking statements before merge. Ships GitHub Actions (ariga/atlas-action). Recent releases added pre-execution policy checks that can allow or deny a migration based on pending files or specific SQL. Supports Postgres, MySQL, SQL Server, ClickHouse, Snowflake, Spanner, Aurora DSQL and others.

tools.name: Flyway
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Versioned SQL migrations with a schema history table, the common choice on JVM services and the tool most teams already have wired into their deploy job.

tools.name: Liquibase
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Changelog-driven migrations with explicit rollback blocks and preconditions, used where the reverse path has to be declared alongside the forward path.

tools.name: Alembic
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Migration tooling for Python services, with upgrade and downgrade revisions. The senior discipline is executing downgrade against a restored copy, not merely writing it.

tools.name: Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL and RDS Blue/Green Deployments
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Managed Postgres, plus Blue/Green Deployments for engine and schema changes with a staged green environment and a fast switchover. Support now extends to Aurora Global Database. Amazon Aurora DSQL is the separate serverless distributed Postgres-compatible offering (CDC to Kinesis went GA in 2026).

tools.name: Amazon ECS and Amazon EKS
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Container runtime. ECS rolling deployments are the concrete reason a mixed-schema window exists at all, since old and new task definitions serve simultaneously. ECS Managed Instances and EKS Auto Mode are the current managed-compute options.

tools.name: AWS Step Functions
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Durable orchestration for long-running backfills, batch settlement pipelines and multi-step migration choreography where each step needs its own retry and idempotency semantics.

tools.name: Amazon DynamoDB
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Single-digit-millisecond key-value and document store for hot paths such as idempotency keys, session state and outbox deduplication alongside the relational store.

tools.name: Azure Kubernetes Service, Azure Container Apps, Azure SQL Database and Azure Cosmos DB
tools.what_it_is_used_for: The equivalent Azure runtime and datastore stack. Container Apps is the serverless container platform (Azure Functions can now run on it), AKS the managed Kubernetes, Azure SQL the managed relational store, Cosmos DB the distributed document store.

tools.name: OpenTelemetry
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Vendor-neutral traces, metrics and logs (all stable across major SDKs) plus Profiles, which entered public alpha in March 2026 and correlates samples to trace_id and span_id. Semantic conventions (1.44.0 line) standardise database, HTTP and messaging attributes. In this story it is what proves which code path served a request, which is the precondition for any zero-traffic claim.

tools.name: Datadog APM
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Distributed tracing, service maps, SLOs and monitors, commonly ingesting OTLP. Used as the deploy-window watchdog and the source of the guardrail metrics a progressive rollout aborts on.

tools.name: Grafana (Grafana Cloud, Tempo, Loki, Mimir)
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Open-source-leaning observability stack: Tempo for traces, Loki for logs, Mimir for long-term Prometheus metrics, Grafana for dashboards and alerting. Prometheus queries here are also what Argo Rollouts AnalysisRuns evaluate.

tools.name: Honeycomb
tools.what_it_is_used_for: High-cardinality, wide-event querying, which is the right tool for questions like "which callers, by service version and merchant id, still read the old column" that dashboards cannot answer. Independent company as of 2026, named a Visionary in the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant for Observability Platforms.

tools.name: Sentry
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Error and exception tracking with release health, used to catch the deserialization and null-handling failures that a mixed-schema window produces in the tail rather than the mean.

tools.name: LaunchDarkly
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Feature flag management, plus Guarded Releases / guarded rollouts (Release Guardian) which measure the new variation against the original using sequential testing and auto-remediate by rolling back when a guardrail metric regresses. The Guardian tier adds release monitoring, error monitoring and session replay. Flags are how the read path is switched independently of the deploy.

tools.name: Argo Rollouts
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Kubernetes progressive delivery controller: canary and blue-green strategies with AnalysisTemplates that spawn AnalysisRuns querying Prometheus or webhooks at intervals, promoting or aborting automatically. Integrates with ingress controllers, service meshes and the Kubernetes Gateway API for traffic shifting.

tools.name: Flagger
tools.what_it_is_used_for: The Flux-family alternative progressive delivery operator for canary, A/B and blue-green on Kubernetes, driven by metric analysis. Actively maintained under fluxcd/flagger.

tools.name: GitHub (Actions, merge queue, repository rulesets, CODEOWNERS, Environments)
tools.what_it_is_used_for: The workflow itself. CODEOWNERS routes review of migrations/ and proto/ to the owners automatically. Rulesets are the current mechanism (up to 75 per repository, multiple can apply and layer, can be disabled without deletion, visible to read-access users) and coexist with classic branch protection rather than replacing it. Merge queue lives in either and requires workflows to add the merge_group trigger, otherwise required checks never report and the merge fails. Environments carry required reviewers, wait timers, deployment branch and tag policies, custom GitHub App protection rules, an admin-bypass toggle, and environment-scoped secrets and variables that are only released once protection rules pass.

tools.name: Azure DevOps (Azure Pipelines, Azure Repos branch policies, GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps)
tools.what_it_is_used_for: The Azure-side equivalent: branch policies rather than rulesets, YAML pipelines with environments and approvals and checks rather than GitHub Environments, and no native merge queue of the GitHub kind. Advanced Security publishes configurable status checks consumable as required branch policies; the AdvancedSecurity-Codeql-Autobuild task is deprecated in favour of buildtype: none and was slated for removal by 1 March 2026, and CodeQL default setup reached GA in July 2026.

tools.name: Apollo GraphOS and Apollo Federation
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Where the team fronts services with a federated graph: subgraph schemas compose into a supergraph schema served by the GraphOS Router. GraphOS schema checks run a build check (does it still compose) followed by operation checks against historical client operation data, so a field removal is judged against traffic that actually exists rather than against the schema alone.

tools.name: Testcontainers
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Real Postgres, Kafka and Azure emulator instances in integration tests, which is what makes it possible to run a forward and reverse migration against production-shaped data in CI instead of against an in-memory fake.

rituals: Pull request review with CODEOWNERS routing: migrations/, proto/ and openapi/ have named owners, so a schema change cannot be self-merged past the person who owns the contract.

Merge queue on the busiest protected branch, with every required workflow carrying the merge_group trigger so checks re-run against the branch as it will actually be after the queue, not as the PR was authored.
Repository rulesets held in version control and applied org-wide, so required checks and review counts do not drift per repository.
Design doc or ADR before any change to a published contract or a shared table, recording the sequence of deploys, who the readers are, and what would make the team reverse.

An expand-and-contract runbook per migration, with the contract step gated on observed evidence (zero reads for N days) rather than a calendar date, and the reverse path executed against a restored snapshot before the forward path merges.
Consumer contract verification in the provider pipeline plus can-i-deploy before release, so the release decision is made against what is deployed rather than what is on main.

Schema compatibility gates: buf breaking in CI and server-side on the BSR, schema registry compatibility level pinned per subject and reviewed when it is loosened, GraphOS operation checks against real client traffic.
Deployment protection rules on production environments: required reviewers, wait timers and branch policies, with environment secrets released only after those rules pass.

Progressive rollout with guardrail metrics and automatic rollback (LaunchDarkly guarded rollouts, or Argo Rollouts AnalysisRuns against Prometheus), so a bad release is bounded by minutes of exposure rather than by how fast someone notices.
On-call rotation with the change author on point during the window, and a deploy freeze convention around the partner's batch schedule rather than around the team's sprint boundary.
Data contracts with downstream consumers, including the batch and partner ones, stating field meaning, units, nullability, ordering guarantees and the notice period required before a shape change.
Post-incident review that ends in a mechanical check, not a reminder: a lint rule, a required status check, a registry compatibility setting.

failure_modes.what_goes_wrong: The backfill misses rows. Either it ran before the two-way trigger existed, so writes landing during the gap only ever hit the old column, or the batching predicate (WHERE new_col IS NULL) races concurrent writers and quietly leaves a tail behind.
failure_modes.why_it_is_silent: Every spot check passes, because the rows people look at are recent and were written after the trigger went in. Counts of non-null values grow monotonically and look complete. Nothing errors, no alert fires, and the gap only becomes visible months later when a reconciliation or a partner dispute reaches back into the affected window.
failure_modes.how_ai_assistance_makes_it_worse: Generated backfill loops look canonical: batched, idempotent, resumable, nicely commented. What they omit is the ordering constraint, that the trigger must exist and be committed before the first batch runs, because that constraint lives in the deploy sequence rather than in the SQL. An assistant asked to write a backfill writes a correct backfill for a table nobody is writing to.

failure_modes.what_goes_wrong: The schema registry compatibility level is set to BACKWARD when the situation required FULL_TRANSITIVE, so removing the old field passes the check while consumers still on the previous schema are live. The producer drops the field, the check is green, and the old consumers start reading a default.
failure_modes.why_it_is_silent: The compatibility check enforces the level you configured, not the level your deployment topology needed, and it reports success. Downstream consumers do not throw: Avro resolution substitutes the schema default, so an amount silently becomes zero or a currency silently becomes the default value, and the aggregates stay plausible.
failure_modes.how_ai_assistance_makes_it_worse: Ask an assistant whether a change is compatible and it will answer against the configured level and return a confident yes. It has no view of which consumer versions are actually deployed, which is the only fact that determines the right answer, so it converts an unanswered question into a green check.

failure_modes.what_goes_wrong: The reverse migration has never been executed. The down block or rollback file is written, reviewed and merged, but it has only ever been read. When it is finally needed it fails, because it drops a column that a later migration renamed, or it takes a lock that cannot be acquired under production traffic, or it assumes a table that has since been partitioned.
failure_modes.why_it_is_silent: Nothing in a normal pipeline runs the reverse path. It passes review because reviewers read it and it looks right, and it accumulates rot with every subsequent migration. The failure surfaces exactly once, during an incident, at the moment the team has least capacity to debug it.
failure_modes.how_ai_assistance_makes_it_worse: Assistants are very good at producing plausible reverse migrations and will produce one for every forward migration on request, which raises coverage and lowers actual safety. The artifact exists, so the box gets ticked and the execution against a restored copy never gets scheduled. Existence of the file becomes the evidence, when the only real evidence is an exit code from a run.

failure_modes.what_goes_wrong: The partner batch job parses positionally. A column is added in the middle of the export row instead of the end, or column order changes because a SELECT * picked up the new physical column. The partner's parser reads currency_code where it expects an amount, coerces it, and produces a settlement file that reconciles to a wrong but plausible total.
failure_modes.why_it_is_silent: The job exits zero. Files arrive on schedule, at the expected size, with the expected row count. There is no schema on a CSV to violate, no consumer-side type check, and no telemetry on the partner's side that the team can see. The discrepancy shows up as a finance query weeks later.
failure_modes.how_ai_assistance_makes_it_worse: The partner job is not in the repository, so it is invisible to any tool that reasons from the codebase. An assistant asked to enumerate consumers of a column returns the services it can grep for, and that list reads as complete. The most dangerous reader is the one that produces no import, no call site and no test.

failure_modes.what_goes_wrong: The decision to contract, to drop the old column, is justified by "no traffic on the old path", but the old path was never instrumented. Only the new code path emits the span attribute that distinguishes them, so the dashboard shows zero old-path reads because there is no emitter, not because there are no reads.
failure_modes.why_it_is_silent: Absence of data renders identically to absence of the behaviour. The graph is flat at zero, which is exactly what success looks like, and every reviewer looking at it draws the same wrong conclusion. This is the failure BrotherSBE's NO-DATA rule exists for: the query returned nothing and nothing was read as a pass.
failure_modes.how_ai_assistance_makes_it_worse: Asked to add instrumentation for a migration, an assistant instruments the code it is currently editing, which is the new path. It rarely goes back to add a counter to the legacy branch it is about to delete, because that looks like pointless work on doomed code. It will then confirm, correctly and uselessly, that the dashboard shows no old-path traffic.

failure_modes.what_goes_wrong: A rounding or unit error in the conversion. Minor-unit conversion multiplies by 100 uniformly, which is wrong for zero-decimal currencies (JPY, KRW) and for three-decimal ones (KWD, BHD), or a half-cent legacy row rounds one way in the backfill and the other way in the application code, so the two disagree by a cent on a subset of rows.
failure_modes.why_it_is_silent: Totals remain the right order of magnitude and most currencies are correct, so aggregate dashboards look normal. Per-currency, per-day reconciliation is the only view that exposes it, and that view usually does not exist until someone builds it specifically for this migration.
failure_modes.how_ai_assistance_makes_it_worse: Multiply-by-100 is the overwhelmingly common pattern in training data and will be produced with high confidence and no caveat. Worse, when asked to verify, an assistant will typically re-derive the figure using the same conversion function it just wrote, producing agreement that proves nothing. A second derivation only counts when it comes from an independent source, such as the CDC stream or the partner's own file.

Attribution nuance, low severity: Flagger is listed with vendor 'Flux project (CNCF)'. Flagger is its own CNCF project living in the fluxcd GitHub org, created at Weaveworks and donated; it is not a component of Flux itself. Weaveworks shut down in Feb 2024, so if the booklet implies vendor backing, that backing is community maintainers, not a company. Prefer 'fluxcd/flagger, CNCF, community maintained'.

stale_naming: GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps has been restructured and rebranded. It is now sold as two separately purchasable products, GitHub Secret Protection for Azure DevOps and GitHub Code Security for Azure DevOps. The draft's entry title is the superseded umbrella name. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/repos/security/configure-github-advanced-security-features and the 2025 sprint 257 release notes.

Forward-looking naming warning for the missing-tools section: dbt Labs no longer exists as a standalone vendor. The Fivetran and dbt Labs merger completed 1 June 2026 and the combined company operates as Fivetran + dbt Labs. The current open-source runtime is dbt Core v2.0, which is the dbt Fusion engine under Apache 2.0. Any booklet mention must use these names, not 'dbt Labs' or 'dbt Cloud' alone. Source: https://www.fivetran.com/press/fivetran-dbt-labs-complete-merger-to-create-the-data-infrastructure-for-trusted-ai-agents

Not stale, checked and cleared: Confluent Stream Governance, Apollo GraphOS Router (correctly using the post-rename name, formerly Apollo Router), Amazon EventBridge, Grafana Tempo/Loki/Mimir, LaunchDarkly guarded rollouts (docs use 'guarded rollouts'; 'Release Guardian' and 'Guardian plan' are the marketing and plan names, both currently live, so the draft's dual naming is defensible).
overclaims: FACTUALLY WRONG. The OpenTelemetry entry claims traces, metrics and logs are 'all stable across major SDKs'. The official status page shows logs are Stable only in C++, C#/.NET, Java and PHP; Beta in Go; and still Development in JavaScript, Python, Ruby, Erlang/Elixir and Swift. Traces and metrics are broadly stable (Rust at Beta). For a booklet whose slogan is evidence before done, shipping a false stability claim about the tool that supplies the evidence is the worst placement possible. Source: https://opentelemetry.io/status/

TOOL CANNOT DO THE JOB ASSIGNED. The draft pins OpenAPI 3.2 and then names Spectral as the mechanical CI gate on that document. Spectral has received minimal investment since the SmartBear acquisition and does not support OpenAPI 3.2: it does not fail on a 3.2 document, it silently ignores 3.2-specific constructs, returning a green check over unlinted content. That is precisely the absent-evidence-read-as-pass failure the NO-DATA rule exists to catch, so the booklet would be recommending an instance of its own antipattern. Its AsyncAPI support is also v2.x only, not v3. Replace with Redocly CLI or vacuum, or keep Spectral and state the 3.2 gap explicitly. Sources: https://github.com/stoplightio/spectral and https://www.speakeasy.com/blog/why-we-built-our-own-openapi-linter/

The Atlas entry says it 'Supports Postgres, MySQL, SQL Server, ClickHouse, Snowflake, Spanner, Aurora DSQL and others' without noting that Snowflake, Spanner, Aurora DSQL, Databricks, Oracle, Redshift and Azure Fabric are Pro-plan (paid) drivers.
