rituals: Example mapping before a story is accepted into a sprint: story on one card, each rule on another, each concrete example under its rule, each unresolved question on a red card. A story still carrying red cards after twenty five minutes is too big or too vague and goes back. The count of red cards is the honest readiness signal, not the estimate.
Three amigos sessions (business owner, engineer, tester) as the gate where acceptance criteria get written, so no criterion is authored alone by the BA and handed over.

Gherkin scenarios committed to the repo next to the code they specify, one feature file per business rule, wired to Cucumber or Reqnroll so an acceptance criterion is a test that can go red rather than a bullet on a page.

Architecture decision records in Markdown in the repo using the MADR template, one file per decision, recording the alternatives that were rejected and what would reverse the call. The BA writes the ones about domain and definition; the engineers write the ones about mechanism.

Pull request review as specification review: the BA reviews PRs that change a business rule, a metric definition, or a public data contract, and their approval is what the BrotherSBE approval gate signs.

A glossary and metric register with one named owner per term, kept as notes with structured properties in the Obsidian vault and surfaced as a table, and mirrored into the repo for anything a build depends on.
A weekly refinement pass over the open-question register, treating every unanswered question as NO-DATA and therefore a blocker rather than an accepted risk.

Data contract review before a producer changes a published dataset: schema, quality expectations, SLA, named consumers, and the deprecation window, expressed as ODCS or dbt model contracts so the review has teeth.

Event storming when a capability is new or badly understood, run in the three named formats in sequence: Big Picture with the business, then Process Modelling, then Software Design with the engineers. Note the official guidance that Big Picture does not transfer well to online delivery and wants people in a room, while Process Modelling and Software Design have officially supported Miro templates for distributed teams.
C4 context and container views maintained as Structurizr DSL or Mermaid in the repo, updated in the same pull request as the change they describe, so the diagram cannot silently rot.

Traceability audit each release: pick a business rule at random, walk rule ID to story to test to merged commit to the deployed change, and treat any broken link as a defect in the process rather than a paperwork gap.

Vault handover hygiene: stable folder and naming conventions, links by note rather than by file path, a maintained map-of-content note per domain, version control via Obsidian Git, and periodic export of anything decision-bearing into the repo. A personal vault only its author can navigate is a single point of failure.

The vault versus repo split, applied deliberately: the vault holds working notes, interview transcripts, half-formed models, open questions and the map of who knows what. The repo holds anything a build, a test or a merge depends on: ADRs, feature files, data contracts, diagrams-as-code, metric definitions. Anything that graduates from thinking to binding moves across, and the vault note is left as a pointer rather than a duplicate.

Post-incident definition review: when a number is disputed in public, the BA runs the same reconciliation loop, and the outcome is either a new example in the feature file or a retired term, never just a Slack explanation.

failure_modes.what_goes_wrong: The same business word is used at two different grains or two different as-of semantics, and the meanings are collapsed into one column, one metric, or one entity. Every consumer's number is individually defensible and none of them reconcile.
failure_modes.why_it_is_silent: Each query returns a plausible number, every test passes because the tests encode the same collapsed assumption, and the discrepancy only surfaces when two people compare figures in a meeting, possibly months after the model shipped. Nothing in the pipeline goes red.
failure_modes.how_ai_assistance_makes_it_worse: An assistant asked to define an entity will synthesise a smooth, agreeable definition from all the inputs it was given, because averaging conflicting sources into fluent prose is exactly what a language model does well. It will not say "these three definitions cannot coexist". It produces a definition that reads like consensus and encodes a defect, then generates the DDL and the tests from that same definition, so the whole stack agrees with itself.

failure_modes.what_goes_wrong: Acceptance criteria are written as prose that sounds testable but has no executable example behind it. The story is marked done when the code compiles and someone eyeballed the screen.
failure_modes.why_it_is_silent: Nothing distinguishes an unexercised criterion from a satisfied one in a tracker. The ticket shows green. Coverage tools report on code paths, not business rules, so a rule never implemented at all leaves no trace.
failure_modes.how_ai_assistance_makes_it_worse: AI is extremely good at producing well-formed Gherkin that never runs, or step definitions whose bodies are empty or trivially assert true. The artefact looks like evidence of verification. This is exactly the case BrotherSBE calls NO-DATA: a check with no execution record is not a pass, but a generated feature file is visually indistinguishable from a passing one until you look at whether it exited zero and took nonzero time.

failure_modes.what_goes_wrong: A metric definition drifts across the places it is written: the dbt model, the semantic layer, a Power BI measure, and a hand-rolled SQL snippet in someone's dashboard. The canonical definition changes and the copies do not.
failure_modes.why_it_is_silent: Each copy keeps working. There is no compile error for a stale duplicate of a business rule. Consumers of the stale copy get no signal that they are downstream of a definition that moved, and lineage tooling that stops at the table boundary will not show a divergence living inside a measure expression.
failure_modes.how_ai_assistance_makes_it_worse: Asked for a number, an assistant will happily write fresh SQL that reimplements the metric rather than routing through the governed definition, because reimplementing is easier than discovering the governed one. Each such answer creates another uncontrolled copy, and the copies multiply at the speed of prompting rather than the speed of code review.

failure_modes.what_goes_wrong: A decision is taken in conversation, implemented, and never recorded. Six months later nobody can say why the system rejects a case it obviously should accept, and the rule gets "fixed" by someone who does not know it was deliberate.
failure_modes.why_it_is_silent: The code is correct and the tests pass. The missing artefact is the rationale, and there is no automated check for absent rationale. The failure surfaces only as a regression introduced by a well-meaning change.
failure_modes.how_ai_assistance_makes_it_worse: An assistant reading only the code will infer intent from implementation and state that inference confidently as the reason. It reconstructs a plausible rationale that was never the actual one, and because the reconstruction is fluent and specific it gets pasted into a document and becomes the record. A wrong recorded reason is worse than an absent one, because it stops anyone from asking.

failure_modes.what_goes_wrong: Requirements traceability decays: rule IDs stop being carried onto stories, stories stop referencing tests, tests stop referencing rules, and the chain from business need to released change breaks in the middle without anyone deciding to break it.
failure_modes.why_it_is_silent: Traceability is a property of links, and a missing link produces no error anywhere. Reports built on those links keep rendering, just with fewer rows, which reads as "less work this quarter" rather than "broken instrumentation".
failure_modes.how_ai_assistance_makes_it_worse: Generated stories and generated tests arrive without the connective metadata, because the linking convention lives in team habit rather than in the code. Volume goes up sharply and the proportion of correctly linked artefacts goes down, so the traceability report degrades fastest exactly when the team is shipping fastest.

failure_modes.what_goes_wrong: A data contract or interface change is deployed with a forward migration that works and a reverse path that was never exercised, or with a deprecation window that exists only in a document.
failure_modes.why_it_is_silent: The forward path is the one CI runs. Nobody exercises the rollback until an incident, at which point it is discovered to be broken while the system is already down. Consumers who were supposed to be notified during the deprecation window were never enumerated, so their breakage arrives as a support ticket.
failure_modes.how_ai_assistance_makes_it_worse: Assistants generate the forward migration readily and the reverse one perfunctorily, often as a comment or a stub, because the forward path is what the prompt asked for. They will also assert that a change is backward compatible based on reading the schema rather than running anything against a restored copy of real data, which is a confident claim with no evidence under it.

failure_modes.what_goes_wrong: Knowledge that exists only in one person's Obsidian vault: the interview that explained why a rule is odd, the map of which stakeholder actually owns a term, the half-finished model holding six months of context. The BA moves teams and it becomes unreadable.
failure_modes.why_it_is_silent: The vault is still there and still opens. Nothing is missing in the file-count sense. What is gone is the navigation: links by file path break on reorganisation, notes assume context the reader does not have, and there is no entry point, so the next person opens it, cannot find the thread, and quietly starts a new vault.
failure_modes.how_ai_assistance_makes_it_worse: AI makes it trivially cheap to generate large volumes of notes, which inflates the vault far past the point where a human can hold its shape, while adding no structure. It also summarises confidently across notes whose provenance and staleness it cannot see, so a superseded definition and a current one get blended into a single fluent answer that the next reader trusts.

verdict.persona: Senior Technical Business Analyst on a delivery team of 8 to 12, sitting between the business owners of a domain and the engineers who build it. The seat owns the definitional layer: what an entity means, which rule governs it, who may change that rule, and how anyone proves later that the shipped system still obeys it. Work is elicitation (interviews, event storming, example mapping), decomposition into slices a squad can build and CI can verify, specification as executable examples rather than prose, and modelling (C4 context and container views, domain and data models, metric and dimension definitions, DMN-style decision tables for the edge cases). On the data side the same person owns the producer/consumer data contract, the semantic layer definitions, and the traceability path from business rule to test to released change. In a BrotherSBE team they run the purpose, process and expression phases and must be satisfied before verification can be written, because a check cannot exist until the rule it checks is unambiguous. They think in the Obsidian vault and bind in the repo, and they treat NO-DATA (a rule with no example, a metric with no owner, an acceptance criterion with no test) as a blocker. PERSONA VERDICT: the persona and the story are sound and correctly pitched at principal level. The "three true definitions of active account" narrative is a genuine senior artefact (three grains, two time semantics, bitemporal treatment, dated deprecation, decision record with the rejected option) and survives refutation unchanged. Every problem found is in the tool list, not in the seat.
invented_or_wrong: Obsidian Web Clipper described as a PAID add-on. Wrong, and the draft marked it 'certain' claiming the names were read directly from obsidian.md. I opened obsidian.md/pricing: it lists exactly four paid items, Sync ($4/user/mo billed annually), Publish ($8/site/mo billed annually), Catalyst ($25 one-time) and Commercial ($50/user/year). Web Clipper is free and is not on that page.

Obsidian 'Enterprise tier' presented as a paid add-on alongside Sync and Publish. An /enterprise page does exist, so this is not fabricated, but it is an enterprise licensing and security offering, not a pricing tier. Separately the draft omits the two items that actually matter to a company of 8 to 12 using Obsidian for work: the Commercial licence and Catalyst.

dbt model contracts described as pinning 'column names and types with constraints such as not_null'. Overstated to the point of being wrong on the common warehouses. dbt contracts reliably enforce column name, order and data type at build time; not_null, primary key, foreign key and check constraints are platform-dependent, and on Snowflake, BigQuery and Databricks several are informational only and are not enforced by the database. A booklet claiming 'this is where your data contract becomes a build failure' must state which constraints actually fail the build on the team's own platform. Confidence high on the direction of the error; the exact per-platform matrix needs checking on docs.getdbt.com before print.

Xray attributed to 'Xpand IT / Xblend'. Wrong vendor as of 2026. Idera, Inc. acquired Xblend Software (Xray, Xporter) on 4 May 2021, and since the 23 January 2025 launch of Sembi, Xray sits inside Sembi, Idera's unified software-quality brand alongside TestRail, Testmo, Ranorex, Kiuwan and PreEmptive. Xpand IT is the consultancy that originally built it and has not been the vendor for five years.

Open Data Contract Standard credited with giving a producer/consumer review 'teeth'. ODCS is a YAML specification and enforces nothing on its own. Teeth come from a runner: the Data Contract CLI, Data Contract Manager, or a CI job that diffs the contract and fails the build. As written this is exactly the document-that-looks-like-a-gate pattern the booklet exists to warn against.

Reqnroll's '5,000+ projects using it by early 2025' is vendor marketing from reqnroll.net presented as a verified fact. The SpecFlow facts around it are solid and worth keeping (end of life 31 December 2024, GitHub projects removed 1 January 2025, no support beyond .NET 7). Drop the adoption number or attribute it to Reqnroll's own announcement.

Great Expectations called 'GX OSS'. The current open-source product name is GX Core, paired with GX Cloud. The draft also describes the pre-1.0 workflow (Expectations grouped into suites run via Checkpoints), which the 1.0 Python API reworked. I am confident on the GX Core naming; I did not re-verify the 1.0 release date or how much suite/checkpoint vocabulary survived, so check docs.greatexpectations.io before printing the workflow sentence.
stale_naming: Obsidian Bases: the draft says 'added as a core plugin in early 2026' and flags the date unverified. It is wrong. Bases shipped in Obsidian 1.9.0 early access on 21 May 2025 and was extended in 1.10.0 on 1 October 2025 (Maps view). By August 2026 it is a mature core plugin, not a novelty. Fix the year and promote the confidence.

GitHub Projects hierarchy view: the draft says 'public preview in January 2026'. Stale by two quarters. Public preview 15 January 2026, improvements 19 February and 5 March 2026, GENERALLY AVAILABLE 19 March 2026 and enabled by default for all new project views, expanding sub-issues up to eight levels deep. Telling a team in August 2026 that it is in preview will make them discount it.

Zephyr Squad is now Zephyr Essential. The draft marked this 'unsure'; SmartBear's own support documentation titles the product Zephyr Essential and describes it as formerly Zephyr Squad / Zephyr for Jira. Promote to certain. Zephyr Scale as the successor to TM4J is also correct.

Structurizr: the draft got this right and it is the one currency check it performed properly. Confirmed on docs.structurizr.com/eol: Lite is replaced by 'local', the CLI by 'pull', 'push' and 'export', the on-premises installation by 'server', all under Structurizr vNext, with Lite, the CLI and on-prem receiving no further updates. Keep the warning against standardising on Lite, and add the licensing shift, because 'server' moves to an open core with closed enterprise extensions, which changes the buy decision for a team of 8 to 12.

dbt Semantic Layer and MetricFlow: the draft labels the re-open-sourcing and the Open Semantic Interchange 'unverified'. Both are real. Snowflake announced OSI on 23 September 2025 with Salesforce, dbt Labs, BlackRock and RelationalAI, added 12 more members including Google and AWS on 13 November 2025, and dbt Labs' commitment to open-source MetricFlow under Apache 2.0 is core to the initiative. Co-leads include Cube, Atlan, Alation, Hex, Omni, Sigma and ThoughtSpot. Promote to certain.

dbt Labs and Fivetran: the 1 June 2026 completion is correct (announced 13 October 2025, closed 1 June 2026, George Fraser CEO, Tristan Handy President). But 'dbt Labs (merger reported complete)' reads as pre-merger for an August 2026 booklet. dbt is now a Fivetran product line, and the dbt Fusion engine is the migration question a data-side BA will actually be asked about.

DataHub: the draft names the vendor 'DataHub'. On datahub.com the copyright is still Acryl Data, Inc. (2026) and the products are named DataHub Core (open source) and DataHub Cloud (commercial). Use those two product names rather than a bare 'DataHub'.

Power BI TMDL: the draft's claim that 'a browser-based TMDL view for published models was announced in 2026' is UNVERIFIED, not refuted. My web-search budget ran out before I could open a Microsoft Learn page, and I have no evidence either way on the date. Flag it for verification rather than printing the year. The datasets-to-semantic-models rename is correct and uncontroversial.

Log4brains and adr-tools: both repositories exist and neither is marked archived, so neither is invented. But adr-tools shows 37 open pull requests against 159 total commits, and log4brains still points users at an @beta install, which reads as dormant. I could not confirm a recent stable release for either. Open the releases pages before recommending them to a 2026 team. MADR 4.0.0 dated 17 September 2024 with full, minimal and bare variants is confirmed correct.
overclaims: 'Column-level lineage' presented as something OpenLineage plus DataHub simply gives you. Coverage is integration-dependent: good for Spark and dbt, patchy to absent for hand-rolled SQL, stored procedures, BI measure expressions, and anything crossing a tool boundary. The draft's own third failure mode admits lineage 'stops at the table boundary' and will not show divergence inside a measure expression, then the tool entry promises the opposite. Pick one and keep the pessimistic version.

Mermaid 'architecture-beta' is sourced from search results only and should be cut. GitHub pins a specific Mermaid version for native rendering and newer diagram types lag or fail there. A BA who commits an architecture-beta block and gets a broken render in the pull request has lost the argument for diagrams-in-git. Recommend flow, sequence and state, which are safe today.

A glossary and metric register in Obsidian credited with producing 'a check in CI that goes red when reality drifts'. Obsidian is a Markdown editor. It enforces nothing and runs no CI. The booklet should say plainly that the vault half of the vault-versus-repo split has zero enforcement power by construction, and that only the repo mirror can fail a build.

'One feature file per business rule, wired to Cucumber or Reqnroll so an acceptance criterion is a test that can go red.' A Gherkin file with generated or empty step definitions passes green, which is the draft's own second failure mode. The ran-gate qualifier belongs in the same sentence: exit code zero AND nonzero elapsed time, plus a deliberate-break or mutation check. Otherwise the tool entry contradicts the failure mode three sections later.

Miro EventStorming templates called 'officially supported'. The Miroverse template page and the eventstorming.com linkage are real and the Brandolini attribution is real, but 'officially supported' overstates the support relationship for a community-contributed template gallery. Soften to 'authored by Brandolini and linked from eventstorming.com'. The Big Picture caveat about in-person delivery is correct and worth keeping.

'Snowflake Semantic Views, Databricks Metric Views, and Cube' bundled into one entry sourced from comparison articles. The products are real, but GA status, supported metric types, and which BI tools can actually read each one differ sharply, and those differences ARE the 'where does the metric legally live and who may change it' decision the entry claims to inform. Verify per-product on vendor documentation or cut the entry. Note the brand is Cube (company Cube Dev), and the more useful fact is that Cube is an Open Semantic Interchange co-lead.

ODCS version number: the docs page references v3.1.0 in passing but does not state a current version, and I could not confirm 3.1.0 is latest as of August 2026. Do not print a version in the booklet unless someone opens the releases page.

Confluence positioned as the home of 'decisions non-engineers must be able to find' while ADRs simultaneously live in the repo. Two homes for one decision reproduces the draft's own fourth failure mode. Apply the same single-source discipline the vault-versus-repo section already states: one binding location, a pointer in the other system, never a duplicate.
missing_obvious_tools: CODEOWNERS plus GitHub branch protection and repository rulesets with required status checks. The single biggest omission. The draft says the BA reviews pull requests that change a business rule, a metric definition or a public data contract, and that 'their approval is what the BrotherSBE approval gate signs', then names no mechanism that makes that review mandatory. CODEOWNERS scoped to the paths holding metric definitions, feature files, data contracts and ADRs, enforced by a ruleset requiring code-owner review, IS the approval gate. Without it the BA's approval is a habit, not a control.
GitHub Actions, or whatever CI the team runs. The booklet is about four mechanical gates before a merge and the tool list contains no CI runner at all.

Azure Data Factory and SAP Integration Suite. The user has since stated these are the team's middleware, and the draft names neither. A Technical BA specifying producer/consumer contracts on that stack works against ADF pipelines and datasets and SAP Integration Suite iFlows, and the reverse-migration and deprecation-window rituals have to be expressible there, not only in dbt. This gap matters more than any other missing tool because it is the team's actual integration layer.

A SQL client and the warehouse itself. The whole 'active account' story is a SQL reconciliation, yet the list aimed at someone who owns metric definitions contains no query tool. Name the warehouse (Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks SQL, or Synapse/Fabric on an Azure stack) and something like DBeaver or DuckDB for local work against extracts.

DMN decision tables and a modeller (Camunda Modeler, or SAP Signavio in SAP-heavy orgs, which is directly relevant given the stated stack). The seniority marker explicitly calls for 'a named rule with a decision table of edge cases' and no decision-table tool appears anywhere. BPMN belongs here too for the process phase.

Pact for consumer-driven contract testing, and Specmatic. The draft's sixth failure mode is entirely about interface changes shipping with an unexercised reverse path and unenumerated consumers, and CDC testing is the standard answer on the service side the way ODCS and dbt contracts are on the data side.

OpenAPI with Spectral for linting, AsyncAPI for event contracts, and Buf for Protobuf breaking-change detection. A BA who owns 'the data contract between producer and consumer' in 2026 owns API and event schemas, not only tables, and 'buf breaking' is the cleanest example in the whole toolchain of a contract that fails a build.

Looker and LookML. The most established governed semantic layer in enterprise BI is absent from a tool list whose central story is a metric definition dispute. Even if the team does not use it, LookML is the reference point for 'the metric lives in one governed, version-controlled place'.

dbt tests, dbt-expectations and dbt docs, plus Elementary for observability. The draft jumps to Soda and Great Expectations while skipping the checks already available in the transformation layer the BA is specifying.

A catalog or governance plane carrying real ownership fields: Unity Catalog, Snowflake Horizon, Microsoft Purview (relevant on an Azure and SAP stack), or Atlan, Collibra, Alation. The rituals demand one named owner per term who 'can be paged', and that ownership has to be queryable, not only a property in one person's vault.

Whiteboarding beyond Miro: Confluence Whiteboards (already licensed if the team has Confluence), FigJam, Mural, Excalidraw, and draw.io or Lucidchart for diagrams a non-engineer will open. Recommending Miro alone ignores that most teams cannot buy a second whiteboard tool.
pytest-bdd or behave. Cucumber and Reqnroll cover JVM, JavaScript, Ruby and .NET; a data-heavy team is on Python and the draft leaves them with no BDD runner.

Obsidian Dataview. Bases is the future but Dataview is what most existing vaults actually run on, and a booklet telling a team to build a glossary and an open-question register in Obsidian should name both and say which to start from.

Slack or Microsoft Teams, and Excel or Google Sheets. Unglamorous but real: the reconciliation in the story happens in a spreadsheet and the deprecation notice goes out in a channel. A tool list with no communication surface and no spreadsheet is not describing the job.

research.persona: Not a person: the operating model that surrounds all five personas. A product-owning team of 8 to 12 (typically 2 to 3 backend, 1 platform/infra, 1 to 2 data engineering, 1 QA/test engineering, 1 technical BA, plus a staff or principal engineer who owns architecture across the group), operating trunk-based on a single GitHub repository or a small set of them. Every change to production reaches it through a pull request against a protected default branch. Ownership is expressed in CODEOWNERS and enforced in repository rulesets. Verification is a CI/CD pipeline whose gates are ordered cheap-to-expensive and whose newest gates run in evaluate/advisory mode before they are promoted to blocking. Durable reasoning lives in a git-backed Obsidian vault: design notes, ADRs, runbooks, data contracts, incident write-ups, benchmark results. Code lives in the repo. The PR is where the two meet, and the health of the whole model is measured by whether that meeting actually happens or is faked. Critically, at this size there is no separate architecture group, no separate QA department and no separate release manager: the same eleven people are the reviewers, the on-call, the data owners and the architects, so every gate they install is a gate they personally have to live with at 2am.
research.seniority_marker:
A team that merely has the tools installed can show you a CODEOWNERS file, a rulesets page, a green pipeline and a vault. A team that runs this well can answer four questions with evidence, on the spot. First: which of your required checks have ever failed and blocked a merge in the last 90 days? Any check that has never gone red is decoration, and they can name the ones they deleted for that reason. Second: show me a PR where a reviewer changed the design, not the code — and they can, because design review happened in the vault before the branch existed, and the PR links to that note. Third: when the vault and the repo disagree, which one is wrong? A mature team has a mechanical answer (a CI check that fails when a migration lands without an updated data contract; a link-checker that fails on a dangling ADR reference) rather than a cultural aspiration. Fourth: who last edited CODEOWNERS, and why? On healthy teams that file changes when the team changes, and the answer is a person and a reorg; on unhealthy teams it was last touched at repo creation and half the handles are people who left.

The deeper marker is that they treat every gate as having a cost they have measured. They know their merge queue's batch size and their pipeline's p50 and p95 duration, they know that the SmartBear/Cisco finding puts useful review at 200 to 400 lines, and they enforce PR size with a warning bot rather than a hard block because they know a hard block gets routed around by squashing. They rolled every new rule out in evaluate mode first, watched Rule Insights, then promoted it — and they have deleted rules that turned out to fire only on false positives. Installing gates is easy. Deleting a gate that is not earning its latency is the senior move.

story.title: One week on an eleven-person ledger team: a partitioning change that crosses four services
story.narrative:
Monday. The principal engineer and the technical BA write a design note in the vault, 10-Design/2026-08-ledger-partitioning.md, before any branch exists: purpose, the process it serves, the architecture delta, the data model, the interface expression, and how it will be verified. No code yet. The note is linked into the weekly architecture review agenda.

Tuesday. The data engineer opens a draft PR carrying the migration and its reverse. CI restores the previous night's anonymised snapshot into an ephemeral database and runs both directions, so 'reversible' is a fact rather than a claim. CODEOWNERS routes db/migrations/** to the data-platform team; because the ruleset requires code-owner approval, the team request is not silently replaced by an individual.

Wednesday. Thirty-minute architecture review. ADR-0042 supersedes ADR-0031. The new fitness function forbidding the reporting service from reading ledger tables directly is added in evaluate mode, not enforcing: they want a week of Rule Insights before it can block anyone.

Thursday. The work lands as a stack of four PRs, each under 300 lines, each reviewed independently. The analyst's restated revenue figure is recomputed by a second person against the same pinned snapshot; the two derivations differ by 0.4 percent on a timezone boundary. That discrepancy is the week's real finding.

Friday. The merge queue batches three of the four. The fourth is ejected: it passed against a stale base and fails the merge_group build. The retro note goes back into the vault, linked from the ADR.
story.why_not_trivial: Nothing here is a feature. The week's output is a reversibility proof, a superseded architecture decision, an advisory-then-enforcing fitness function, a second independent derivation that caught a 0.4 percent error, and a merge-queue ejection that proves the queue is doing the job branch protection alone cannot. Each of those requires someone who can hold the system's invariants in their head: knowing that a migration that only runs forward is untested, that an ADR without a superseding link rots, that a new rule enforced on day one gets bypassed rather than obeyed, and that a figure derived once is not a figure. A junior can open the PRs. Nobody junior decides that the fitness function waits a week, or that a 0.4 percent gap is the finding rather than a rounding annoyance.

tools.name: GitHub repository rulesets
tools.what_it_is_used_for: The current mechanism for protecting branches, replacing classic branch protection in practice. Unlike classic rules, where only a single branch protection rule applies at a time, multiple rulesets layer and aggregate on the same branch. Rules include: require a pull request before merging, require status checks to pass (strict or loose), require code owner review, dismiss stale approvals, require approval from someone other than the last pusher, require linear history, require signed commits, require deployments to succeed, require code scanning results, require code quality results, restrict code coverage (public preview), require merge queue, and restrict file paths/extensions/size. Each ruleset has an enforcement status of Active, Evaluate or Disabled: Evaluate runs the rules and reports to the Rule Insights page without blocking merges, which is the native advisory-then-enforcing rollout path. Bypass is per-actor (users, teams, GitHub Apps) rather than the classic default where repo admins bypass everything unless 'do not allow bypassing' is ticked.

tools.name: CODEOWNERS
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Maps path patterns to owning individuals and teams so review is requested automatically. Its documented limits are the load-bearing part for a team this size: the file must be under 3 MB or it is not loaded at all; gitignore-style negation (!), character ranges ([ ]) and escaped # are NOT supported; the LAST matching pattern wins and only that pattern's owners are requested, so a broad catch-all placed late silently disables everything above it; paths are case-sensitive; the file must exist on the pull request's BASE branch; code owners are not automatically requested on draft pull requests; owners must have write permission and an owning team must be visible and hold write permission even if every member already has it individually; and any file matching no pattern gets no reviewer requested at all. CODEOWNERS expresses ownership, it does not enforce policy: enforcement only exists if a ruleset also requires code owner review.

tools.name: Required reviewer rule (repository rulesets)
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Went generally available on 17 February 2026. Configured inside rulesets rather than in a file, it requires a specified number of approvals (0 to 10) from up to 15 designated teams for changes matching file patterns, and unlike CODEOWNERS it supports negation to exclude paths such as tests. GitHub's own framing is that it augments CODEOWNERS rather than replacing it: CODEOWNERS for ownership and individual routing, this rule for centrally enforced approval policy on sensitive paths (migrations, IaC, auth, pipeline definitions). This closes the most common gap at 8 to 12 people, where CODEOWNERS names a team but nothing guarantees that team's approval.

tools.name: GitHub merge queue
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Prevents the semantic conflict where two PRs each pass against a stale base and break the trunk when combined. It builds temporary branches named gh-readonly-queue/{base_branch}/... containing the base plus each queued PR in order, and tests the batch. CI must explicitly subscribe to the merge_group event (on: [pull_request, merge_group]) or checks never run and the queue stalls. A failing PR is ejected and the remaining temporary branches are rebuilt without it. The 'only merge non-failing pull requests' setting decides whether a PR that individually failed can ride in a group whose final member passes. It is a repository-level rule and cannot be enabled on a classic branch protection rule that uses a wildcard (*) in the branch name pattern. Requeueing or jumping positions triggers full rebuilds, so the queue trades merge latency for trunk safety.

tools.name: gh-stack (GitHub stacked pull requests)
tools.what_it_is_used_for: GitHub's native stacked-PR workflow, in private preview from 13 April 2026 and public preview from 30 July 2026, installed as a CLI extension (gh extension install github/gh-stack) and also usable from github.com, the mobile app, and coding agents. Each PR in a stack targets the layer below it rather than main, so a large change becomes an ordered series of small independently reviewable PRs. It provides a stack map, auto-rebase and retarget when lower layers merge, partial merges (land one layer or the whole stack), and works with existing branch protections and required checks. Merge queue support was still rolling out progressively at public preview. Directly relevant because it is the mechanism by which a team keeps PRs inside the 200 to 400 line review-effectiveness window without stalling the author.

tools.name: Graphite
tools.what_it_is_used_for: The established commercial stacked-PR toolchain that predates GitHub's native support: CLI-first stack management, a review web UI optimised for reviewing a stack layer by layer, and its own merge queue. Teams already on it in 2026 are weighing it against gh-stack. Open-source alternatives in the same space are ghstack (Meta, commit-oriented), git-spice, Sapling/ReviewStack, git-branchless and Git Town, plus git rebase --update-refs built into Git 2.38+ which handles the mechanical part of restacking with no extra tooling. I did not independently verify Graphite's 2026 pricing or its reported acquisition, so treat commercial details as unconfirmed.

tools.name: GitHub Actions
tools.what_it_is_used_for: The pipeline itself for most teams of this size. Relevant mechanics: required status checks are matched by check NAME, so renaming a job silently un-requires it (a classic way a gate quietly disappears); the merge_group trigger must be added for merge queue; and organisation- or enterprise-level rulesets can require specific workflows to pass, pinned to a branch, tag or exact SHA, so the gate definition itself cannot be edited away in the PR being gated. That last property is what makes a gate genuinely non-bypassable rather than merely present.

tools.name: Obsidian
tools.what_it_is_used_for: The team's knowledge vault: plain Markdown files with YAML frontmatter on local disk, which is precisely why it can be a git repository. Teams keep design notes, ADRs, runbooks, data contracts and dictionaries, incident write-ups, on-call handovers and benchmark results here. Since version 1.9 (May 2025) the core Bases plugin turns collections of notes into filterable database views backed by a .base file and the notes' own YAML properties, with Table and Cards layouts (List and Map added in 1.10) — which is how a vault gets a live ADR index or an open-decisions board without a third-party plugin. Note that 1.9 also removed the singular property forms tag, alias and cssclass in favour of the plural list forms, a breaking change for older vault templates.

tools.name: Obsidian Git (community plugin, by Vinzent03)
tools.what_it_is_used_for: The usual way a team vault gets synced through a git remote instead of a proprietary sync service: automatic commit-and-sync on a timer, auto-pull on startup, a Source Control view for staging and committing, a History view, a diff view, and editor gutter signs for changed hunks on desktop. The failure surface matters for a team: it needs a native git install on desktop, and mobile support is explicitly documented as very unstable because it falls back to isomorphic-git — no SSH authentication, no submodules, no rebase merge strategy, and crashes or buffer overflows on large repositories depending on device RAM. Teams that put the vault behind a real remote get real merge conflicts in prose, which is a feature (it forces reconciliation) and a support burden (non-engineers on the team will need help resolving them). Obsidian's own paid Obsidian Sync is the alternative when the vault contains material that should not sit in the code remote.

tools.name: Structurizr (DSL, Lite, on-premises, cloud)
tools.what_it_is_used_for: The reference 'diagrams as code' implementation of the C4 model by its creator. A single text model in Structurizr DSL, version-controlled next to the code, renders multiple consistent views (system context, container, component) rather than a pile of hand-drawn diagrams that disagree with each other. Structurizr Lite runs locally against a workspace file for browsing and authoring; on-premises and cloud variants serve a team. This is the practical answer to the diagram-drift problem: the diagram is generated from a model that lives in the repo and is reviewed in the same PR as the change it describes.

tools.name: ArchUnit
tools.vendor: ArchUnit / TNG Technology Consulting (open source, Apache 2.0)
tools.what_it_is_used_for: The canonical way to turn an architecture decision into an executable fitness function on the JVM: rules such as 'no class in the persistence package may depend on the ui package' or 'the reporting module may not import ledger internals' run as ordinary tests in CI and fail the build when the architecture drifts. Equivalents exist per ecosystem (NetArchTest for .NET, Spring Modulith's verification and Documenter for modular monoliths, plus dependency-cruiser or import-linter in the JS/Python worlds). The rule of thumb from the evolutionary-architecture literature is that every important architectural decision should have a corresponding fitness function, because decisions without one degrade silently. In practice this is the mechanism that keeps an ADR from becoming a historical document.

tools.name: MADR (Markdown Architectural Decision Records) and Log4brains
tools.what_it_is_used_for: MADR is the widely used ADR template, available in full and minimal variants each in annotated and bare form, requiring no tooling at all — you paste it into a Markdown file in the repo. Log4brains is a Node-based CLI that scaffolds and numbers ADRs, tracks supersession, and publishes the ADR directory as a searchable static site. Worth flagging: the original adr-tools bash CLI by Nat Pryce has not been maintained for a long time, so a team standardising in 2026 should not build on it. For a team of this size the whole practice can be two things: a numbered directory of MADR files in the repo, and a Bases view in the vault that indexes them by status.

tools.name: Open Policy Agent / Conftest
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Policy as code for the parts of a PR that are configuration rather than application code: Terraform plans, Kubernetes manifests, workflow definitions, Dockerfiles. The mechanic that matters organisationally is the warn-versus-deny split in Rego: a new policy ships as warn (visible, non-blocking), the team is notified and given a communicated deadline, then the rule is promoted from warn to deny and becomes the enforcement point that fails the build. This is the same advisory-then-enforcing pattern as GitHub's ruleset Evaluate mode, applied one layer down, and it is why new gates get adopted instead of routed around.

tools.name: Danger JS
tools.what_it_is_used_for: Runs after CI and automates the review conventions that are tedious to police by hand but easy to state as rules: PR is too large, no test file touched alongside a source change, changelog not updated, migration added without a corresponding data-contract note, PR description missing a link to a vault design note. It writes structured feedback onto the PR itself. The important design choice at this team size is that Danger comments (soft) while rulesets block (hard): conventions that are still being negotiated live in Danger, and only graduate to a required check once the team stops arguing about them.

tools.name: Backstage
tools.vendor: Cloud Native Computing Foundation (originated at Spotify)
tools.what_it_is_used_for: An open framework for internal developer portals, currently a CNCF incubating project. Its Software Catalog registers services with their owners and dependencies, and TechDocs renders Markdown docs stored alongside the source. Relevant here mainly as the alternative shape of the knowledge layer: teams that outgrow an Obsidian vault, or that need ownership metadata to be machine-readable and joined to the deployment graph, move to a catalog. At 8 to 12 people it is usually more platform than the team needs, and an Obsidian vault plus CODEOWNERS covers the same ground with far less operational cost. Adoption figures circulating for 2026 (thousands of organisations, majority framework share) come from vendor and community summaries rather than an audited source.

rituals: Design before branch. A design note lands in the vault (purpose, process, architecture, data, expression, verification) and gets a reader before a branch exists. This is where design review actually happens; PR review is far too late to change a design and everyone knows it, which is why 'LGTM' on an architecturally wrong PR is so common.

Weekly architecture review, 30 minutes, fixed slot, agenda built from open ADRs in the vault. Decisions leave the room as a numbered MADR file in the repo with an explicit status and, where a previous decision is overturned, a supersedes link in both directions.

Every ADR that constrains code gets a fitness function, or it gets an explicit note saying why it cannot have one. An unenforceable decision is recorded as unenforceable rather than pretended to be enforced.

New gates ship in advisory mode first: GitHub ruleset Evaluate status, or a Conftest warn rule, or a Danger comment. A stated promotion date, Rule Insights or warn-rate reviewed on that date, then promoted to Active/deny or deleted. Nothing goes straight to blocking.

PR size discipline: target the 200 to 400 line window the review literature supports, enforced by a bot comment rather than a hard block, with stacked PRs (gh-stack or Graphite) as the escape hatch so authors are not forced to choose between a reviewable PR and forward progress.

A pickup-time norm rather than a review-time norm: PRs get a first response within a few business hours, tracked as a team metric. Pickup time is typically the largest single component of PR cycle time, so this is the highest-leverage number the team controls.

Reviewer routing by GitHub team review assignment (round robin or load balance, with busy members skipped) on top of CODEOWNERS, so review load is distributed rather than landing on the same two people. Note the interaction: the team request is replaced by individuals unless code-owner review is actually required by a rule.
Migrations are reviewed as forward-and-reverse pairs, both executed in CI against a restored snapshot of production-shaped data, in an ephemeral database that is destroyed afterwards.

Any figure that leaves the team (a restated metric, a capacity number, a cost projection) is derived twice, by two people or two code paths, against the same pinned snapshot. Disagreements are logged in the vault even when the cause turns out to be trivial.
Runbooks live in the vault and are exercised, not just written: the on-call handover at the end of each rotation names which runbooks were used, which were wrong, and which PR fixed them.
Incident write-ups are blameless, land in the vault within a week, and each action item is either a PR link or an explicit 'accepted risk' with a named owner.
CODEOWNERS is reviewed whenever the team composition changes, and the file itself is code-owned so a change to ownership requires the same approval as a change to code.

Data contracts (schema, semantics, freshness expectation, owner) live in the vault next to the pipeline that produces them, and a CI check fails a PR that changes a table's schema without touching its contract note.
The vault and repo are reconciled on a schedule: a link checker for dangling ADR and design-note references, and a periodic sweep for notes whose subject no longer exists in the codebase.

failure_modes.what_goes_wrong: Rubber-stamp review. Approvals are given without the reviewer building a real model of the change: a diff scroll, a scan of the test file names, LGTM. The required-approvals rule is satisfied, the PR merges, and the review adds no defect detection at all. It compounds with PR size, because the review literature (the SmartBear study of a Cisco team) puts useful defect discovery at roughly 200 to 400 lines and a review pace under about 500 lines per hour, and a 1,400-line PR simply cannot be reviewed at that quality by anyone.
failure_modes.why_it_is_silent: Every observable signal looks identical to a genuine review. The approval count is met, the check is green, the cycle time is good — in fact a rubber-stamping team scores BETTER on pickup time and review time than a rigorous one, so the metrics dashboard actively rewards the failure. The only distinguishing evidence is the absence of review comments that changed the change, and nobody tracks absences. The defect surfaces weeks later in production, by which point it is attributed to the author, not to the review.
failure_modes.how_ai_assistance_makes_it_worse: The asymmetry is the whole problem: AI makes authoring far faster than reviewing, and reviewing someone else's code is already harder than writing your own. DORA's 2026 work reports that around 90 percent of technology professionals now use AI at work while about 30 percent of developers report little to no trust in AI-generated code, and finds that AI adoption raises delivery throughput while also raising delivery instability. So the queue of PRs per reviewer grows, each PR is larger, and the reviewer's confidence in the author's own understanding drops. Then AI review bots are added to relieve the load, and their plausible, confidently-worded summaries become a second rubber stamp: the human reads the bot's approval rather than the diff. Worst of all, AI-generated code is locally idiomatic and reads as correct, which strips away the surface cues (odd naming, inconsistent style, obviously copied blocks) that used to make a reviewer slow down.

failure_modes.what_goes_wrong: The vault goes stale and quietly diverges from the repository. Design notes describe an architecture that was abandoned three sprints ago, the runbook references a service that was renamed, the data dictionary lists columns that were dropped. The vault stops being the place decisions live and becomes a museum, so people stop reading it, so it degrades faster.
failure_modes.why_it_is_silent: There is no build that fails when a note is wrong. Prose has no compiler and no test suite. Documentation maintained outside the development workflow drifts by default, and the drift is invisible precisely because the vault is a separate repository from the code with no mechanical link between them: nothing in the PR that renamed the service knows a note mentions it. Worse, a stale note is more dangerous than a missing one, because a missing note prompts someone to ask, while a confidently wrong note gets believed and acted on — typically at 3am by whoever is on call.
failure_modes.how_ai_assistance_makes_it_worse: Two ways. First, AI makes it trivially cheap to generate volume, so the vault fills with plausible generated notes that nobody has verified, diluting the notes that were written by someone who actually knew, and making the stale-to-fresh ratio much worse. Second and more serious: AI coding agents READ the vault as authoritative context. A stale note stops being passively wrong and becomes an active instruction — the agent reads the abandoned design, implements against it, produces code that is internally coherent and confidently explained, and the reviewer's context for judging that code is the same stale note. The error is laundered through a machine that cannot signal its own uncertainty, and it arrives looking like a well-reasoned implementation of a decision the team never made.

failure_modes.what_goes_wrong: Checks stay advisory forever. A gate is introduced in GitHub ruleset Evaluate mode, or as a Conftest warn rule, or as a Danger comment, with an honest intention to promote it to blocking once the noise settles. Nobody sets a date, or the date passes during an incident week. Eighteen months later it is still advisory, still emitting warnings nobody reads, and the team believes it is protected by a control that has never once prevented a merge.
failure_modes.why_it_is_silent: The check is present in every configuration file and appears on every PR, so an auditor, a new joiner, or the team's own leadership sees a policy that exists. The status is green-adjacent and the annotation scrolls past. Nothing distinguishes 'this gate has never fired' from 'this gate fires and everyone complies' without deliberately querying Rule Insights or the warn history. The related silent variant is worse: a required status check is matched by NAME, so renaming or refactoring a CI job removes the requirement entirely and the branch is now unprotected with no error anywhere. Both failures are only visible to someone who asks the negative question — which of our controls has never blocked anything?
failure_modes.how_ai_assistance_makes_it_worse: The whole point of an assurance layer around AI-assisted work is that the machine cannot vouch for itself, so the gate has to be mechanical. An advisory gate is exactly the gate an AI agent will step past: it reads the warning, notes it as non-blocking, and proceeds — often summarising the run as successful because the exit code was zero. Agents also generate far more configuration churn, including edits to workflow files and job names, so the rename-breaks-the-required-check failure fires much more often. And an agent asked to make CI pass will, reasonably and without malice, take the shortest available route: relax the assertion, mark the test skipped, add the path to an ignore list. Every one of those moves is legitimate-looking in a diff and turns a real gate into an advisory one without anyone deciding to.

failure_modes.what_goes_wrong: CODEOWNERS decays until it routes review to nobody or to the wrong people. Handles belong to people who left. A team was renamed and the entry no longer resolves. Someone appended a broad catch-all pattern at the bottom of the file, and because the LAST matching pattern wins and only its owners are requested, every specific ownership rule above it silently stopped applying. New directories match no pattern at all, so no review is requested for them. Or the owning team lost repository write permission (or is a secret team), so GitHub cannot request it even though the entry looks correct.
failure_modes.why_it_is_silent: CODEOWNERS fails open, not closed. An unmatched path does not error — it simply requests no reviewer, and the PR proceeds under the generic approval rule with whoever happened to be around. A shadowed rule produces no warning in the PR. Case sensitivity means a path that looks right can be inert. If the file exceeds 3 MB it is not loaded at all and ownership silently vanishes repo-wide. And because the file only takes effect from the PR's BASE branch, a fix merged to main does not protect a long-lived release branch. The team's belief in the ownership map stays intact because the map is never tested; the first real test is an incident where the person who should have reviewed a change finds out afterwards that it shipped.
failure_modes.how_ai_assistance_makes_it_worse: AI-assisted work spreads changes across more of the tree in a single PR than a human would naturally touch: a request to add a feature comes back with edits to the service, the migration, the IaC, the CI workflow and the docs. The proportion of a diff that falls outside anyone's declared ownership rises sharply, and every unowned file is a file with no expert reviewer. Agents also readily create new directories and new modules, which by definition match no existing pattern. And when asked to fix a CODEOWNERS file, a model will happily produce syntax that looks right but is not supported — negation with !, character ranges with [ ], escaped # — all of which are silently skipped as invalid rather than rejected loudly.

failure_modes.what_goes_wrong: Gate theatre in the pipeline: the CI/CD stages are ordered badly or scoped wrongly, so the expensive, meaningful checks (integration against a restored snapshot, migration reversibility, contract tests, performance budgets) are pushed to a nightly or post-merge job while the merge-blocking set is lint, unit tests and a coverage floor. The team says 'CI is green' meaning the cheap third of it passed.
failure_modes.why_it_is_silent: The green tick on the PR is the same shape regardless of what it covered. Pushing slow checks off the merge path is usually a defensible latency decision made once, in a hurry, by one person, and never revisited; there is no artefact recording that the merge gate was narrowed. Post-merge failures land in a channel nobody owns, get triaged as flakes, and get muted. The merge queue variant is subtler still: if CI does not subscribe to the merge_group event, the batch build never reports and the queue either stalls or, misconfigured, lets a batch through that was only ever validated as individual PRs against stale bases.
failure_modes.how_ai_assistance_makes_it_worse: AI raises merge throughput, which raises pipeline cost and duration, which creates direct pressure to trim the merge-blocking set — the failure is a rational response to a load increase the tooling caused. It also raises the flake rate, because more concurrent changes mean more interaction failures, and flakes are the standard justification for demoting a check to non-blocking. Most damaging: an agent reporting on its own work will describe a pipeline run as passing based on the exit code, without distinguishing which stages actually executed. A check that was skipped because a path filter did not match, or that exited zero in one millisecond because it found nothing to do, is indistinguishable in a summary from a check that ran for four minutes and genuinely verified something. Absent evidence gets reported as passing evidence, which is exactly the thing an assurance layer has to refuse to do.

verdict.persona: The operating model wrapper: an 8-to-12 person product-owning team (backend, platform, data engineering, QA, technical BA, plus a staff/principal architect) working trunk-based on GitHub PRs with a git-backed Obsidian vault. Adversarial verdict: the tool inventory is unusually clean (no fabricated products found), but it carries one confabulated author attribution, three stale vendor/ownership facts, one mis-dated statistic, several capability overclaims, and a domain-sized hole where the data engineering and middleware toolchain should be, including the stack this team actually runs (Azure Data Factory and SAP Integration Suite).
invented_or_wrong: MISATTRIBUTION (hard error, must not ship). Log4brains is credited to 'Thomas Dussouillez'. No such maintainer exists. Log4brains is by thomvaill (Thomas Vaillant): https://github.com/thomvaill/log4brains . The name in the draft appears confabulated.

MISATTRIBUTED VENDOR. 'Open Policy Agent (CNCF) / Styra' is wrong as of Aug 2026. Styra wound down in August 2025; Apple hired the OPA creators and core team (an acquihire, not a company acquisition). OPA is a CNCF GRADUATED project (graduated 29 Jan 2021), not merely 'a CNCF project'. Conftest lives in the open-policy-agent org and is actively maintained (v0.69.0, released 2026-08-03). Correct attribution: 'Open Policy Agent / Conftest — CNCF graduated, community-maintained'. Sources: https://www.cncf.io/projects/open-policy-agent-opa/ , https://github.com/open-policy-agent/conftest/releases

MIS-DATED STATISTIC. The draft says 'DORA's 2026 work reports around 90 percent... and about 30 percent...'. Those figures belong to the DORA State of AI-assisted Software Development 2025 report (adoption 76% in 2024 to 90% in 2025; 30% report little-to-no trust). The cited page https://dora.dev/insights/balancing-ai-tensions/ attributes them to the 2025 report itself. No 2026 DORA report backs these numbers.

UNSOURCED NUMBERS. The required reviewer rule entry states '0 to 10 approvals from up to 15 designated teams'. The GA changelog does not state those bounds and I could not source them on any GitHub page. Everything else in that entry is verbatim-accurate (GA 17 Feb 2026; negation with ! added since public preview; GitHub's own words: 'augments CODEOWNERS files but doesn't replace them'). Drop the two numbers or cite them.
MINOR MISATTRIBUTION. 'ghstack (Meta, commit-oriented)' — ghstack is Edward Yang's tool from the PyTorch ecosystem, not a Meta product. Soften the vendor claim.

MINOR FACTUAL SLIP. Obsidian Bases: the Map layout is not a plain 1.10 built-in, it requires Obsidian 1.10 PLUS the separate official Maps plugin (github.com/obsidianmd/obsidian-maps). Also 1.9.0 shipped Table only — the 1.9.0 changelog says 'more view types' were still on the roadmap — so Cards arrived in a later 1.9.x, not at 1.9. The rest of the entry is exact, including the breaking change: 'We have officially removed support for the properties tag, alias, cssclass in favor of tags, aliases and cssclasses.'
stale_naming: Graphite is no longer an independent vendor: Cursor (Anysphere) acquired it in December 2025, product continuing to operate. The draft hedges this as an 'unconfirmed reported acquisition' — it is confirmed. Should read 'Graphite (Anysphere/Cursor)'. This matters editorially: a 2026 team choosing between gh-stack and Graphite is now choosing an AI-editor vendor's product.
Styra no longer exists as OPA's commercial vendor (wound down Aug 2025). Any sentence pairing 'OPA' with 'Styra' is a year stale.

dbt Labs no longer exists as an independent vendor: the Fivetran / dbt Labs merger completed 1 June 2026 (announced 13 Oct 2025), CEO George Fraser, President Tristan Handy. dbt Core v2.0 ships the Rust-based Fusion engine under Apache 2.0. The draft never names dbt, but any addition must use current ownership.

Azure Data Factory is still the correct product name, but Microsoft Learn (page updated 2026-08-05) now carries a standing tip that 'Data Factory in Microsoft Fabric is the next generation of Azure Data Factory' and directs new users to Fabric with a documented ADF-to-Fabric upgrade path. A 2026 booklet that says 'ADF' without acknowledging the Fabric successor will read as out of date to this team. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/introduction

SAP Integration Suite is the current umbrella name (the former SAP Cloud Platform Integration / SAP CPI now sits inside it as the Cloud Integration capability). UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION — sap.com returned HTTP 403 to my fetch and the web-search budget was exhausted. Flagging so the booklet author confirms the current capability names before print rather than trusting my memory.

Classic branch protection should be named consistently as 'classic' throughout, since the draft's own (correct) merge-queue claim depends on the distinction: merge queue cannot be enabled on a classic branch protection rule that uses a wildcard in the branch name pattern.
overclaims: Ruleset 'Evaluate' mode is presented as the universal, native advisory-then-enforcing rollout path, and the entire rituals section leans on it. It is gated in a way the draft never mentions. The general docs.github.com pages ('About rulesets', 'Creating rulesets for a repository') list only Active and Disabled as enforcement statuses; Evaluate is a first-class status on the Enterprise Cloud pages and appears on the general page only buried in the metadata-restrictions subsection. Rulesets as a whole require GitHub Team or Enterprise. Verify against the team's actual plan before the booklet promises it. Add the sharp edge the draft omits: rules in Evaluate or Disabled rulesets are NOT returned by the REST API's active-rules endpoint, so any script auditing 'what protects this branch' is blind to them — which is itself an instance of the draft's own 'checks stay advisory forever' failure mode.

'Organisation- or enterprise-level rulesets can require specific workflows to pass, pinned to a branch, tag or exact SHA, so the gate definition itself cannot be edited away in the PR being gated.' Overstated. Tamper-resistance only holds when the required workflow lives in a DIFFERENT repository and is pinned to a SHA rather than a branch. Same-repo and branch-pinned, it remains editable. As written it promises non-bypassability the mechanism does not deliver alone.

'Restrict code coverage' is listed beside mature rules as if generally available. It is real and currently public preview, but conditional: GitHub's docs gate it on the repository having GitHub Code Quality enabled AND coverage data actually being uploaded. Same caveat applies to 'Require code quality results'.

CODEOWNERS and drafts: 'code owners are not automatically requested on draft pull requests' is accurate but framed as a permanent absence. Owners ARE requested when the draft is marked ready for review, so the real failure is a timing gap. As written, a reader could conclude drafts never route at all.

Merge queue branch naming is presented as universal. GitHub's docs present gh-readonly-queue/{base_branch} specifically as what THIRD-PARTY CI providers must watch; an Actions-based team subscribes to the merge_group event instead. Correct in substance, misleading as instruction.

gh-stack is built into a ritual without its disqualifying limits: all branches must be in the SAME repository (no cross-fork stacks), it is not supported in GitHub Desktop, and the docs still say 'This feature is in public preview and subject to change.' Merge queue support was still rolling out at public preview, which the draft does say. A booklet should not hang a standing practice on a preview feature without stating that.

'A CI check fails a PR that changes a table's schema without touching its contract note' is asserted as an existing ritual with no mechanism named anywhere in the tool list. Either name the tool or mark it as a pattern the team must build — otherwise the booklet is doing exactly what BrotherSBE says never to do, treating absent evidence as a pass.
missing_obvious_tools: The team's actual middleware is absent entirely. The session context states this team runs Azure Data Factory and SAP Integration Suite as middleware, and neither appears anywhere in the research. This is the biggest practical gap: ADF pipelines are JSON artefacts with first-class Git integration and documented CI/CD via Azure DevOps and GitHub (ARM template publish from the adf_publish branch), which is precisely where the booklet's four merge gates would attach. SAP Integration Suite iFlows have their own transport and lifecycle model that does not naturally sit inside a GitHub PR at all — that friction deserves a named treatment, not silence.

Schema migration tooling — the migration gate ('forward and reverse both run against a restored copy') names no migration tool at all. A principal in this seat uses Flyway, Liquibase, Atlas (Ariga), Alembic, golang-migrate or Sqitch, and the choice determines whether a reverse migration is even expressible. Atlas specifically does declarative diffing plus destructive-change linting in CI, which is the mechanical form of the claim being made.

Ephemeral database provisioning — the Tuesday story restores 'the previous night's anonymised snapshot into an ephemeral database' with no mechanism. Testcontainers is the standard answer; database branching (Neon, PlanetScale) and pg_restore into a throwaway container are the others. Without one, the gate is aspiration.

The data engineering toolchain is missing wholesale, despite the audience explicitly including senior ICs shipping data products end to end: dbt (dbt Core v2.0 / Fusion, Fivetran-owned) with its tests, contracts and source freshness; an orchestrator (Apache Airflow 3, Dagster, Prefect, or ADF triggers for this team); and a data-quality gate (Soda Core, GX Core). A booklet naming Structurizr and ArchUnit but not one data tool will not survive contact with the data engineers.

Data and API contract tooling — dbt model contracts, the Open Data Contract Standard (Bitol, Linux Foundation), Buf for protobuf breaking-change detection, oasdiff or Spectral for OpenAPI, Pact for consumer-driven contract tests, Schemathesis. These are what make the contract ritual mechanical.
Table-format time travel — Apache Iceberg or Delta Lake snapshot IDs are how a 'pinned snapshot' is actually pinned. The second-derivation gate depends on pinning and never says how.

Lineage and catalog — OpenLineage (+ Marquez), DataHub, OpenMetadata, Unity Catalog, or Microsoft Purview for an Azure-centric team. These are the mechanical answer to the draft's own question 'when the vault and the repo disagree, which one is wrong?' for data assets.

Supply-chain evidence — the approval gate is 'a signed trailer' and the thesis is evidence, yet Sigstore/cosign, gitsign, GitHub artifact attestations and SLSA provenance are all absent. These turn a signature from decoration into something verifiable.

Merge-path security and dependency gates — CodeQL, Semgrep, Trivy, gitleaks, and Dependabot or Renovate. Every team this size runs at least two as required checks, and bot-PR churn is a primary driver of the merge-queue behaviour the story dramatises.
pre-commit — the cheap end of the 'cheap-to-expensive gate ordering' the whole persona rests on. Plus SQLFluff for the SQL half.

Affected-target selection — Nx, Turborepo or Bazel. The cheap-to-expensive ordering claim and the p50/p95 pipeline numbers in the seniority marker are unreachable in a monorepo without a mechanism for running only what changed.

Infrastructure as code itself — Conftest is described as evaluating 'Terraform plans' but Terraform/OpenTofu is never listed, nor Atlantis or Spacelift for plan-gating inside the PR, nor Bicep for an Azure team. The policy layer is named without the thing it polices.
Mergify (and Aviator) — the realistic merge-queue option for teams that cannot use GitHub's; Mergify shipped GitHub-ruleset required-reviewer support in June 2026.
Backstage peers, if that comparison is kept — Cortex, OpsLevel, Port.

concepts.for_persona_or_act: backend engineer, splitting an implicit-currency money column across four readers

concepts.for_persona_or_act: backend engineer, designing the order of change so each intermediate state stands alone
concepts.diagram_type: deploy staircase with a revert arc on every tread except one, and an evidence gate feeding the last tread
concepts.what_it_shows: Five deploy steps rising left to right, each with a curved arc returning to the previous state, and a final tread with no arc. An evidence box beneath the last tread feeds it: zero reads over one full billing cycle. The picture is about which states you can leave.
concepts.why_this_shape: Reversibility is a property of the edge between states, not of a state, so the mark that matters is an arc that is present four times and absent once. A before and after diagram has exactly two states and therefore cannot express the idea that the intermediate states are the design.

Riser lines connect the right edge of each tread to the left edge of the next (from Tn right end down-up to Tn+1 left end). Tread labels 11px inside: '1 add columns', '2 backfill batches', '3 dual write', '4 read new path', '5 drop old column'. Revert arcs: for T2, T3, T4, T5 draw a quadratic arc from the tread's top-left (x, y) up and back to the previous tread's top-right, with an arrowhead at the previous tread, stroke-width 1. Only one arc carries a label: on T3's arc at 236,150, 'revert' (11px). Left note at 30,286, 11px opacity 0.65: 'every rung ships alone'.
concepts.caption_argument: Order is the design. Four of these steps can be undone by a deploy, one cannot, and the only thing standing between the two is a measurement that has to be instrumented before it can be believed.

concepts.for_persona_or_act: infrastructure, what a required check actually proves
concepts.diagram_type: identical surface over divergent substrate: one row of four indistinguishable green checks, each opened out into what actually happened underneath
concepts.what_it_shows: Four required checks reporting pass. Beneath the fold: one ran four minutes over 812 files, one was skipped by a job-level condition, one was posted straight to the statuses endpoint by a token with no code access, one exited zero over zero matched files. Three of the four carry a NO-DATA marker.
concepts.why_this_shape: This is not a comparison between two configurations, it is a claim that one visible signal has many invisible causes. The shape has to be one row that is deliberately, boringly uniform, with a rule under it and four different stories below. The uniformity of the top row is the argument; symmetry does the work that colour is not allowed to do.

Four check glyphs at cx = 110, 250, 390, 530, cy=48: circle r13 plus a check polyline inside, all drawn identically at stroke-width 1.5. Identical caption under each at y=76, centred, 11px: 'required check, pass' (repeated verbatim four times). Horizontal rule y=94, x 40 to 600, stroke-width 1, opacity 0.5. Label at 40,112, 11px opacity 0.65: 'what actually ran'. Four boxes y=124 h=118 w=120, x = 50, 190, 330, 470. Box 1 solid outline; boxes 2, 3, 4 dashed (4,3). Three text lines each, 11px, 16px leading, starting y=148: box1 'ran 4m 12s' / '812 files' / '1 finding'; box2 'job-level if:' / 'skipped' / '0s'; box3 'POST /statuses' / 'repo:status token' / 'no code read'; box4 'exit 0' / '0 files matched' / '0.4s'. Short 12px stem from each box top centre up to its check glyph. Small hollow square 9x9 at the bottom-left inside boxes 2, 3, 4 at y=228 with label 'NO-DATA' at 11px to its right.
concepts.caption_argument: The merge rule matches a name against a conclusion. It has no opinion about whether anything was examined, which is why three of these four ticks are the absence of evidence wearing the costume of evidence.

concepts.for_persona_or_act: infrastructure, deriving the exact identity a trust policy should accept
concepts.diagram_type: nested aperture rings of admitted identities, with a claim-format union band across the cutover date
concepts.what_it_shows: Four concentric regions, each one a candidate subject condition, with a count of how many identities it admits and a single dot at the centre marking the one you meant. Beside it, the two live claim formats either side of 15 July 2026 and the bracket showing the policy must accept both before it can narrow.
concepts.why_this_shape: Over-permission is a containment relationship, so the honest picture is a set diagram: the wildcard is not the opposite of the exact condition, it is a superset of it, and that is invisible in a two-column layout. Concentric rings also let the reader see that every tutorial answer is the outermost ring without the drawing having to say so.

Counts right-aligned inside the right edge of each ring at 10px: '~1400', '~310', '2', '1'. Filled dot r3.5 at 215,155 with leader line to 300,206 and label 'the identity you meant' (11px). Right panel: vertical rule x=470 from y=46 to y=250, label at top 470,38 centred '15 Jul 2026' (11px).
